Rate adjustments may be made only on these grounds: the resident's written approval; an emergency; a physician's order; or 30 days' written notice of an increase in operating cost. The Administrator gives the 30-day notice in writing and keeps a copy. A rate increase is never applied without one of these grounds.

The agreement also states any money or property given to the operator by the resident; the offer to place SSI or HR personal allowance funds in a facility account (see RR-05); the bed-reservation charge, which may not exceed the basic rate; the terms and grounds for termination; the prorated refund of advance payments; the final accounting on discharge; and the annual medical evaluation.

For ALR residents, the Case Manager confirms before signature that the services listed in the residency agreement match the ISP developed under ARD-03, and that any additional services and their charges are specified in the agreement.

The Administrator does not accept an agreement that waives any provision required by 18 NYCRR 487.5(d). Any such waiver language is void and is removed. The facility does not offer or sign life-care contracts.

For SSI recipients, the Business Office confirms the basic rate charged does not exceed what the current SSI Congregate Care Level 3 allows after the personal needs allowance ($1,688 less $262, or approximately $1,426 as of January 1, 2026). The Business Office updates this each year when OTDA publishes new amounts.
The Business Office records any deposit or advance payment on a dated receipt that is given to the resident, shows the amount and purpose, and is also recorded in the resident's payment account.
The resident or representative and the Administrator sign and date the agreement. The resident receives a complete signed copy. The original is placed in the resident record (REC-01).

When a resident leaves, for any reason, the Business Office calculates a prorated refund of any advance payments and prepares a final accounting. The refund and accounting are delivered at discharge, and the date is documented. See RR-05 for return of money and property.

The Administrator posts the starting monthly rate, rent range, the approved agreement and fee summary in the ALR, and publishes the same on the facility's website, as required by Public Health Law §4656. The Administrator updates them within 10 business days of any change and reports annual quality measures to DOH as that law requires.
The Administrator compares the agreement template and posted prices against the current regulations at least annually, and whenever DOH issues new guidance. Revisions are controlled under GOV-04.

Staff must never pressure an applicant to sign immediately, waive a right, or make a payment not shown in the agreement. The Administrator investigates reports of such conduct and handles them under STF-07.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the DOH agreement and addenda are used unaltered, signs agreements, gives rate-change notices, ensures price posting and website accuracy.
Explains the agreement, confirms ISP and agreement services match, and keeps signed copies.
Receipts payments, computes SSI-eligible rates, prorated refunds and final accounting.
Reviews and signs the agreement, pays charges as stated, and gives required notices.

documentation: Signed admission/residency agreement and addenda in each resident record
DOH approval of the agreement template (Part II)
Schedule of optional services and charges
30-day rate-increase notices or written approvals
Deposit and payment receipts, refund calculations and final accounting
Posted ALR price information and website screenshot with date
Annual agreement-template compliance review

policies.title: Resident Funds, Personal Allowance Accounts and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: All residents, with emphasis on SSI and Home Relief/Safety Net recipients; Business Office and Administrator (Adult Home, Enriched Housing, ALR, EALR, SNALR, ALP)
policies.purpose: To protect residents' personal funds and belongings by making a personal allowance account available, keeping accurate records, and returning money and property when a resident leaves.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] offers each SSI or Home Relief (HR) recipient, or the resident's representative payee, the opportunity to place personal funds in a facility-maintained account, and records whether the offer is accepted or rejected. A signatory who declines must comply with the personal allowance requirement. The facility uses the DOH forms, keeps separate payment and personal fund accounts and a current inventory of property held, posts the times residents may access their personal allowance accounts, and on discharge or transfer gives a final written statement and immediately returns all money and property.

definitions.definition: The amount a resident who receives SSI or HR keeps for personal needs after the facility's charges. For 2026 the SSI personal needs allowance is $262 per month.
A facility-maintained account, separate from operating funds, holding a resident's own money at the resident's request.
The record of charges and payments between the resident and the facility.
The DOH form on which the facility records the offer to maintain a personal allowance account and the resident's or signatory's acceptance or rejection.
A person or organization appointed to receive and manage a beneficiary's benefits on the beneficiary's behalf.

procedures: At admission and before the first payment is due, the Business Office offers each SSI or HR recipient, or the representative payee, the chance to have the facility keep personal funds in a personal fund account. The offer is explained in plain language and in the resident's preferred language.

The Business Office completes the Statement of Offering (DSS-2853), recording whether the offer was accepted or rejected, with the date, and obtains the signature of the resident or representative. If the resident declines to sign, the staff member notes that on the form.

If a signatory declines the account, the Business Office informs the signatory in writing that the signatory must comply with the personal allowance requirement, and documents the conversation. The Administrator reviews any declined offer within five business days.

If the account is accepted, the Business Office opens a separate personal fund account for the resident. Resident funds are never mixed with the facility's operating funds, and are never used for facility expenses or charges not authorized by the resident in writing.

The Business Office keeps the DOH forms current: the Personal Allowance Summary (DSS-2855), the Personal Allowance Ledger, and the Inventory of Resident Property (DSS-3027). Every deposit and withdrawal is recorded on the ledger on the day it occurs, with date, amount, purpose, balance and signatures.

The Business Office keeps a payment account and a personal fund account for each resident who uses the service, plus a current inventory of any property held for the resident, as required for facility records.

The Administrator posts the schedule of times residents may access their personal allowance accounts in a conspicuous public place. The schedule allows reasonable access, and the Business Office also gives money in an emergency at other times where possible.

A resident or authorized representative may withdraw funds on request during the posted schedule. The staff member counts the money with the resident, the resident signs the ledger, and a second staff member witnesses the transaction when staff handle cash.

At admission, the Case Manager and the resident list personal property the resident brings, on the Inventory of Resident Property (DSS-3027), for items the facility agrees to hold or that are of value. The resident signs, and the list is updated whenever items are added or removed.
Staff do not accept, hold or borrow resident money or property except through these procedures. Staff do not take gifts, loans or gratuities from residents under STF-07.

The Business Office gives each resident with an account, or the representative, a written statement of the account at least quarterly, and at any time upon request. The Administrator reviews each ledger against bank statements at least monthly and signs the review.

If the facility becomes aware of missing funds or property, staff report to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates the same day, notifies the resident and representative, and reports any suspected theft or financial exploitation under SAF-01 and SAF-02.

On discharge or transfer, including death, the Business Office gives the resident or the legally authorized person a final written statement of the account and immediately returns all money and property held, obtaining a signature on receipt. For deceased residents, funds and property are released only to the person legally entitled to them, and the Administrator documents the release.
The Administrator reviews the funds process for compliance at least once per year and presents the results to the QA/QI Committee under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees resident funds handling, posts the access schedule, performs monthly reconciliation review and investigates losses.
Makes the offer, completes DOH forms, maintains the ledgers and accounts, and processes withdrawals and final accounting.
Helps complete the property inventory and supports residents in understanding their accounts.
Do not hold or handle resident money outside these procedures and report any loss immediately.

documentation: Statement of Offering (DSS-2853) for each SSI/HR recipient
Personal Allowance Summary (DSS-2855) and Personal Allowance Ledger
Inventory of Resident Property (DSS-3027) with updates
Payment account and personal fund account records
Posted schedule for access to accounts
Monthly reconciliation reviews
Final written statements and receipts on discharge or transfer
Loss or theft investigation files

policies.title: Advance Directives and Health Care Decision-Making
policies.applies_to: All residents and applicants; Administrator, case manager, direct-care staff and any nurse or home care agency staff working in [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's right to make his or her own health care decisions is respected, that residents are told about advance directives, and that a resident's wishes and designated representative are known and honored when the resident cannot decide.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects the right of every resident to manage his or her own affairs and to choose his or her own medical providers. Residents are presumed able to make their own decisions unless a physician, PA or NP determines otherwise through the process required by law. The home does not require a resident to sign, change or revoke an advance directive as a condition of admission or continued residency, and does not treat residents differently based on whether they have one. The home asks about a resident's representative and any advance directive at the admission interview and on the medical evaluation (DSS-3122). It keeps current copies where staff can find them quickly in an emergency. It honors valid directives under New York's Health Care Proxy Law, the Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (MOLST) program and the Family Health Care Decisions Act. Staff do not give legal advice and do not complete a directive for a resident. Statutory references in this policy are general and are to be confirmed by [AGENCY NAME]'s legal counsel before adoption.

definitions.definition: A signed and witnessed document in which a competent adult names another person (the agent) to make health care decisions if the adult loses the ability to decide.
A written statement of a person's wishes about future medical treatment.

Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment: a physician-, NP- or PA-signed medical order form for seriously ill residents, including resuscitation and intubation preferences. Where it applies, it is honored by EMS and health care providers.
A medical order, signed by a authorized practitioner, directing EMS and other providers not to attempt resuscitation outside a hospital.

The person identified by the resident, or authorized by law, to receive notices and assist with decisions, such as a health care agent, guardian, or family member, as identified at the admission interview.
A person authorized by New York law to make certain health care decisions for a patient who lacks capacity and has no health care agent.

procedures: At the pre-admission administrator interview, the Administrator or designee asks the applicant whether he or she has a health care proxy, living will, MOLST, non-hospital DNR order, guardian, power of attorney or other representative. The answers are recorded in the interview summary.

The Administrator or designee reviews the DSS-3122 medical evaluation for representative information and any physician notes on capacity, and records the name and contact information of each representative on the resident's face sheet.

At or before admission, the case manager gives the applicant written information on health care proxies and advance directives, and offers to help the resident contact a physician, attorney or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman about completing one. Staff do not complete, witness or sign directives for residents and do not act as a resident's health care agent.
The home documents that the information was offered. It does not require a directive as a condition of admission and does not discourage one.

The case manager files copies of every directive, MOLST and DNR order in a designated, clearly labeled section at the front of the resident record. A flag on the face sheet shows that a directive exists and where it is kept.

The case manager places a current MOLST or non-hospital DNR in a location agreed with the resident, if the resident has chosen to have one, so staff and EMS can find it quickly. Staff are told the location at orientation.

The case manager reviews each resident's directive status at the annual reassessment, after any hospital stay, and on a significant change in condition. The case manager confirms that the contact information of the agent is current and asks the resident whether his or her wishes have changed.

If a resident wants to change or revoke a directive, staff tell the case manager at once. The case manager helps the resident notify his or her physician and agent, replaces the copies in the record, and removes superseded documents from the active section (but retains them per REC-01).

If the resident appears to lack capacity to make a decision, the Administrator or case manager asks the resident's physician to assess capacity and documents the request. The home does not make a capacity finding itself.

If a resident lacks capacity, the case manager identifies the agent named in any health care proxy and contacts that person. If there is no agent, the case manager asks the resident's physician or the hospital to identify the lawful surrogate. The home does not choose a decision-maker on its own.

In an emergency, staff call 911 and begin first aid as required. When EMS arrives, staff give EMS any non-hospital DNR order or MOLST immediately and send a copy with the resident, along with the face sheet and medication list, to the hospital.
Staff must not withhold emergency response or first aid because of a belief about a resident's wishes. Only a valid written order authorizes withholding resuscitation.

The Administrator notifies the resident's physician and the resident's representative of any dispute about a resident's wishes. The Administrator contacts the Ombudsman or counsel as needed and documents what was done.
The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at orientation and at least annually (see STF-03), including where directives are kept and how to give them to EMS.

The Administrator reviews a sample of records at least every six months through the QA process (GOV-05) to check that directive information is current and findable, and reports results to the committee.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the policy is followed, handles disputes and capacity concerns, arranges training and audits.
Offers information, records representative and directive status, files documents, updates at reassessment and change of condition.
Know where directives are kept, give them to EMS, respond to emergencies, report resident questions or changes in wishes to the case manager.
Determines capacity, writes MOLST and DNR orders, and documents on the DSS-3122.
Confirms statutory references and advises on unusual decision-making situations.

documentation: Admission interview summary showing the directive and representative questions asked and the answers
DSS-3122 medical evaluation with representative information
Copies of health care proxy, living will, MOLST, non-hospital DNR order, guardianship papers and POA in the resident record
Record of advance directive information offered to the resident
Annual reassessment and change-of-condition notes on directive status
Capacity assessment requests and physician responses
Training attendance records and QA audit results

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality, HIV-Related Information and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and students of [AGENCY NAME]; all resident, applicant and employee records
policies.purpose: To protect the confidentiality of resident, applicant and employee information, including HIV-related information, while keeping records available to staff who need them for routine and emergency care.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to confidential treatment of their personal, social, financial and health records. [AGENCY NAME] keeps records so that resident privacy is protected but staff who need the information for routine and emergency services can reach it. Confidential HIV-related information about residents, employees, volunteers, applicants and prospective residents is protected as required by New York law and the Department's adult care facility regulations. Records the operator is required to keep are never posted or made available to the public. Information is released only as permitted by law or with a valid written authorization. To the extent [AGENCY NAME] or any of its health care providers is a HIPAA covered entity, it follows the federal privacy rules, including the minimum-necessary standard, a notice of privacy practices, and administrative safeguards. The incident-report process (SAF-02) includes the resident's own version of events unless the resident objects.

definitions.definition: Individually identifiable health information, in any form, relating to a resident's health, care or payment for care.
Information that identifies, or could reasonably identify, a person as having had an HIV test, as having HIV infection or illness, or as being a contact of such a person.
Using or disclosing only the least amount of information needed for a purpose.
A signed, dated, written permission from the resident or lawful representative that states what information may be released, to whom, and for what purpose.
The person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to oversee privacy and confidentiality; [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME / TITLE].

procedures: The Administrator designates a Privacy Officer in writing. Unless another person is named, the Administrator is the Privacy Officer.

Resident, employee, volunteer and applicant records are kept in locked cabinets or access-controlled electronic systems. Active resident records are kept in a staff-only area that is available to authorized staff at all hours for emergencies. Records are never left open in public areas, hallways or dining rooms.

Staff may access only the information they need to do their jobs. The Administrator assigns access in writing by position and reviews the list at least every six months and when staff leave or change role.

Staff do not discuss resident information in hallways, the dining room, elevators, on personal phones or social media, or with anyone not involved in the resident's care. Staff do not take photographs or videos of residents without the resident's written consent.
Each employee signs a confidentiality statement at hire and again at annual training, and receives training on this policy at orientation and at least annually (see STF-03).

HIV-related information on residents, applicants, employees and volunteers is kept in a separate, locked file or restricted electronic area. Only staff with a legal need to know have access. Any release requires a specific signed release meeting New York requirements or a disclosure otherwise allowed by law. The Administrator reviews each request and consults counsel when uncertain.

Medical, financial and personal information is released to outside parties only with the resident's or lawful representative's written authorization, or where the law permits or requires it. Examples are reports to DOH, the Justice Center, Adult Protective Services, public health authorities, EMS and treating providers in emergencies, and the Ombudsman as provided in RR-03.

Records the operator is required to keep are never posted or made available to the public. Only the documents listed in REC-03 are posted. No posting may contain a resident's name or health information.

Where [AGENCY NAME] or its providers are covered by HIPAA, the Privacy Officer maintains a Notice of Privacy Practices, gives it to each resident at admission, obtains acknowledgment, and posts or makes it available as required.

Residents or their representatives may ask to see or get a copy of their records. The Privacy Officer responds within a reasonable time, consistent with law, and documents the request, the response, and any denial and its reasons.
Residents may ask for corrections to their records. The Privacy Officer reviews each request, makes the correction or documents why not, and tells the resident.

Resident version of incident events: the incident report includes the resident's own version of what happened unless the resident objects. The staff member offers this opportunity and records any objection.

Staff who learn of a possible breach (lost records, misdirected fax or email, unauthorized access, or release of HIV-related information) report it to the Privacy Officer on the same shift. The Privacy Officer investigates within one business day, limits further disclosure, notifies the resident and any required agencies as the law requires, and documents corrective action.
Any staff who improperly access or disclose confidential information are subject to discipline up to termination (see STF-07).
The Privacy Officer reports privacy incidents and audit results to the QA committee at least every six months (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Controls access, releases information, investigates breaches, handles requests for records and corrections, and trains staff.
Obtains authorizations, keeps resident files organized and secure, and explains confidentiality to residents.
Protect all resident, applicant and employee information, and report suspected breaches immediately.
Protect resident information under written agreements with the home.

documentation: Written designation of Privacy Officer
Staff access list and review dates
Signed employee confidentiality statements
Signed authorizations and releases
HIV-related information release log
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments (if applicable)
Records request, amendment and denial logs
Breach and privacy incident investigations
Training records and QA minutes

policies.title: Nondiscrimination, Mobility Impairment Accommodation and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All applicants, residents, visitors and staff; Administrator, case manager, admissions and direct-care staff
federal: ADA Title III, 42 USC 12181 et seq.
policies.purpose: To ensure that no person is excluded or treated unfairly because of disability, mobility impairment, language or other protected status, and that applicants and residents can understand the information they are given.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not exclude an applicant because of a mobility impairment and makes reasonable accommodations consistent with federal, state and local law. The home does not discriminate in admission, services, discharge or treatment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, age, disability or any other protected status. Residents' civil and religious liberties are not infringed, and residents may choose their roommates. When an applicant or resident is sight- or hearing-impaired or cannot understand English or printed material, the home arranges the interview and explains the agreement, resident rights and facility information in a way the person can understand. Direct-contact staff must speak, read and write English and also speak the predominant language of residents. Admission decisions are based on whether the home can lawfully meet the person's needs (see ARD-01 and ARD-04), not on a protected characteristic.

definitions.definition: A change to a rule, policy, practice, service or physical setup that lets a person with a disability use and enjoy the home's services, unless it would be an undue burden or fundamental alteration or conflict with a legal limit on who the home may serve.
A condition that limits a person's ability to walk or move about independently, including use of a wheelchair, walker or cane.
Limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.

A person who is competent to interpret accurately and impartially in both languages, including sign language. A resident's family member or another resident is not used as an interpreter except at the resident's own informed request when no other option is available in an emergency.

procedures: The Administrator posts and provides a nondiscrimination statement stating that the home does not discriminate and how to complain (see RR-02 and REC-03).

At first contact, staff ask each applicant whether he or she needs an interpreter, large print, sign language, written materials in another language or another accommodation, and record the answer on the inquiry log.

The Administrator arranges needed language or communication help before the admission interview. Options include a qualified interpreter, a telephone or video interpreter service, a sign-language interpreter, large-print or read-aloud materials, or other aids. [AGENCY NAME] pays for these services and does not charge the applicant or resident.

Staff conduct the interview and explain the admission agreement, resident rights statement, facility rules and the Ombudsman/legal-services sheet in a way the applicant understands. The Administrator documents the method used and confirms understanding in the interview summary.

The Administrator does not deny admission or retention based on mobility impairment alone. The Administrator evaluates, with the case manager, whether the person's needs can be met with reasonable accommodations such as room placement, assistive devices, grab bars, ramps, transfer help or modified procedures. The Administrator records the evaluation.

Where the home determines it cannot meet a person's needs, the denial is based on the specific legal admission or retention criteria (see ARD-01, ARD-04), not on disability or a protected characteristic. The reason is explained to the applicant in writing, and the applicant is helped to find an alternative where appropriate.

Residents may ask for an accommodation at any time. Staff refer all requests to the case manager, who records the request, consults the resident, decides within [number of days, recommended 5] business days, and records the outcome and reasons. Denials are reviewed by the Administrator.

Staff honor residents' civil and religious liberties, including attendance at religious services or choosing not to attend, and do not require any resident to take part in a religious activity. The case manager helps arrange access to clergy or services on request.

The case manager asks about roommate preferences at admission and when a vacancy occurs. Residents choose their roommates where space allows, and the home does not assign roommates based on a protected characteristic. Roommate conflicts are handled through the case manager and documented.

The Administrator ensures direct-contact staff can speak, read and write English and speak the predominant language of the residents. If residents speak a language not spoken by enough staff, the Administrator assigns bilingual staff or arranges an interpreter and notes the plan.

Staff must never use language, jokes, or gestures that demean residents or others, or refuse care based on a protected characteristic. Violations are reported to the Administrator and may result in discipline (see STF-07). Staff report suspected abuse through SAF-01.
Staff receive training on this policy at orientation and at least annually, including how to use interpreter services and respond to accommodation requests (STF-03).
Residents or applicants who believe they have been discriminated against may use the grievance process (RR-02) or contact the Ombudsman (RR-03) or DOH. No retaliation is allowed.
The Administrator reviews accommodation requests, interpreter use, denials of admission and complaints at least every six months with the QA committee (GOV-05) to look for patterns.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nondiscrimination, arranges accommodations and interpreters, decides admission questions, and reviews data.
Records and decides accommodation requests, supports communication needs, handles roommate preferences.
Treat everyone respectfully, use interpreter services, and report accommodation requests and discrimination concerns.
Reviews trends and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Nondiscrimination statement as posted
Inquiry log recording communication needs
Interview summaries noting language or communication method used
Interpreter or translation service records
Accommodation request log and decisions
Written denial letters with specific legal reasons
Roommate preference records
Training records and QA minutes

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening, Medical and Mental Health Evaluation, and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: All applicants and prospective residents; Administrator, case manager, admissions staff and consulting clinicians of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To admit only people whose physical, psychological and social needs [AGENCY NAME] can lawfully and safely meet, through a documented screening process that includes a medical evaluation, an administrator interview and, where indicated, a mental health evaluation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only after determining that the program can meet that person's needs. The determination is based on a current medical evaluation (DSS-3122 or approved substitute), an interview by the Administrator or designee with the applicant and the applicant's representative, and a mental health evaluation if the applicant has a known or suggested chronic mental disability. The home never admits or retains a person who falls within the categories excluded by 18 NYCRR 487.4 (see ARD-04), and never exceeds its certified capacity. For ALR, the case manager meets the prospective resident before admission and explains the basic ALR, EALR and SNALR levels of service. Applicants receive the required documents and may review the most recent DOH inspection report.

definitions.definition: The New York State medical evaluation form (or a DOH-approved substitute) used for admission and annual evaluations.
A documented interview conducted by the Administrator or designee with the applicant and the representative before admission.
The maximum number of residents allowed by the operating certificate.
Assisted Living Residence; Enhanced Assisted Living Residence; Special Needs Assisted Living Residence, with the service levels the facility is approved to provide.
An adult home designated by DOH under rules that require a DOH pre-admission screening for serious mental illness.

procedures: Staff answer inquiries using the inquiry log. They give general information only and make no promise of admission before screening is complete.

The Administrator checks the current census against the certified capacity on the operating certificate before scheduling an admission. The home does not admit anyone if the admission would exceed certified capacity.

The Administrator sends the applicant or the representative a request for the DSS-3122 (or approved substitute) to be completed by the applicant's physician, PA or NP. It must be based on a physical examination performed within 30 days before the date of admission.

If the applicant has a known or suggested chronic mental disability (for example from history, diagnosis, medications, or referral information), the Administrator arranges a mental health evaluation by a qualified professional before admission and reviews the findings.

If the applicant comes from a hospital, nursing home or psychiatric facility, the Administrator obtains the referral source's statement of significant conditions and reviews it with the medical evaluation.

If [AGENCY NAME] is designated a transitional adult home, the Administrator obtains the DOH pre-admission screening for serious mental illness before admission. If it is not so designated, this step does not apply, and the Administrator notes this in the file.

The Administrator or designee interviews the applicant and the representative in person or by approved means, using interpreter or accommodation services as needed (RR-08). The interview covers the applicant's needs, abilities, preferences, finances, representatives, expectations and the services [AGENCY NAME] can and cannot provide.

At or before the interview, staff give the applicant a copy of the admission agreement, the resident rights statement, the facility rules, and the Ombudsman and legal-services information sheet. Staff tell the applicant he or she may review the latest DOH inspection report, and provide it on request. Staff record these actions.
The Administrator completes a written interview summary with the date, the people present and a summary of what was discussed, and signs it.

For ALR, the case manager meets the prospective resident before admission, explains the basic ALR, EALR and SNALR levels of service available, and begins the pre-admission evaluation described in ARD-02. The case manager records the meeting.

The Administrator, with the case manager and the reviewing clinician, compares the applicant's documented needs against the exclusion criteria in ARD-04 and the services the home is approved and staffed to provide, including nursing coverage and home care arrangements (HCS-03).

The Administrator records a written admission decision. If the person is accepted, the decision states the determination that the home can meet the person's physical, psychological and social needs and any conditions such as arranging a home care agency.

If the applicant is not accepted, the Administrator gives a written explanation of the reason and, where appropriate, helps the applicant identify other options. A denial is never based on a protected characteristic (RR-08).
Admission takes place only after the agreement is reviewed and signed (RR-04), and the evaluation, interview summary and all other required admission documents are in the file.
The case manager gives the resident a copy of the signed documents, introduces the resident to staff, and opens the individualized service plan process (ARD-03).
The Administrator audits all new admission files within 30 days of admission and reports the results of the audit to the QA committee at least every six months (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Makes the admission decision, conducts or oversees the interview, verifies capacity and criteria, and signs the written summary.
Meets the prospective ALR resident, explains service levels, coordinates the evaluations and starts the service plan.
Performs the examination and completes the DSS-3122.
Completes the mental health evaluation when indicated.
Log inquiries, assemble packets, and make sure required documents are provided.

documentation: Inquiry log
DSS-3122 (or approved substitute) with examination date within 30 days before admission
Mental health evaluation, if applicable
Referral source statement of significant conditions, if applicable
Administrator interview summary with date and attendees
Record of documents given to the applicant, including the DOH inspection report availability
Case manager's pre-admission meeting note
Written admission or denial decision
Census versus certified capacity check
Signed admission agreement

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Annual Reassessment
policies.applies_to: All residents; case manager, Administrator, nursing and direct-care staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's needs, interests and strengths are identified before admission and re-evaluated at least every 12 months and whenever the resident's condition changes, so services and retention decisions stay accurate.
policies.policy: The case manager identifies and evaluates each resident's needs, interests and strengths before admission and at least every 12 months using the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form. A medical evaluation, and a mental health evaluation where required, is repeated at least every 12 months and on a change in condition. The home uses the DOH Personal Data Sheet (DSS-2949) as required. The home helps residents obtain the evaluations. Assessment findings are used to update the individualized service plan and to decide whether the resident can still be retained (ARD-04).

definitions.term: Personal data and resident evaluation form
definitions.definition: The DOH-prescribed form used by the case manager to assess the resident's needs, interests and strengths.
The Personal Data Sheet mandated for adult care facility residents.
A significant or abrupt change in a resident's physical, mental, behavioral or functional status, or a hospitalization.
A formal re-evaluation at least every 12 months or earlier on a change in condition.

procedures: Before admission, the case manager meets the applicant and representative and completes the DOH personal data and resident evaluation form, covering needs, interests and strengths. The form is filed in the record at admission.
On or before the day of admission, the case manager completes the Personal Data Sheet (DSS-2949), checks that the information is complete, and files it in the record.

The case manager creates a reassessment calendar listing every resident's admission date. Each resident's reassessment is due at least every 12 months from the previous one. The case manager schedules it at least 30 days ahead.

At least 30 days before each annual medical evaluation due date, the case manager notifies the resident and representative and asks the resident's chosen physician, PA or NP to complete a new DSS-3122. The case manager helps with transportation or scheduling when asked (DL-04) and offers help to obtain any required mental health evaluation.

The case manager completes the annual reassessment using the DOH form. It includes interviewing the resident, speaking with the representative if the resident agrees, and consulting direct-care staff, nursing and home care agency staff.
The case manager updates the Personal Data Sheet (DSS-2949) as information changes and at each annual reassessment.

Staff report changes in condition to the case manager and the nurse on the same shift (HCS-04). The case manager arranges an updated medical evaluation and, if required, a mental health evaluation, and starts a reassessment earlier than the 12-month date.

After any hospital, rehabilitation or psychiatric stay, the case manager reviews the discharge information and reassesses the resident before or on return, and reviews it with the Administrator to confirm that the home can still meet the resident's needs.

The Administrator reviews each reassessment and medical evaluation against the retention limits in ARD-04. If the resident's needs appear to exceed what the home may lawfully serve, the Administrator starts the alternative-placement process in ARD-04 and ARD-05 immediately.

The case manager updates the individualized service plan within [number of days, recommended 14] days of the reassessment and reviews it with the resident (ARD-03). The case manager records the resident's participation and any disagreement.
The case manager gives the resident a chance to review the results of the assessment and records the discussion. If the resident disagrees, the disagreement is noted in the record.
The case manager reports overdue evaluations weekly to the Administrator. The Administrator takes action on any evaluation that is more than 30 days overdue, and records it.
The Administrator reports the percentage of timely reassessments and medical evaluations to the QA committee at least every six months (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Completes pre-admission and annual evaluations, tracks due dates, helps residents obtain required evaluations, updates the DSS-2949 and the service plan.
Reviews reassessment findings against retention limits and follows up on overdue items.
Reports health changes and contributes to the reassessment.
Report changes in condition, behavior or function immediately.
Completes DSS-3122 at least every 12 months and on a change in condition.

documentation: DOH personal data and resident evaluation form (pre-admission and annual)
Personal Data Sheet DSS-2949, with updates
Annual DSS-3122 and mental health evaluations, where required
Reassessment calendar and overdue-evaluation reports
Notes of requests for evaluations and help provided
Change-of-condition reassessment notes
Updated service plan and resident review note
QA reports on timeliness

policies.title: Case Management and Individualized Service Plan
policies.applies_to: All residents; case manager, Administrator, nursing and direct-care staff, and contracted providers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide case management to every resident and to ensure each resident has a written individualized service plan (ISP) that is coordinated, current and based on his or her needs and choices.
policies.policy: Case management is a required service. For ALR residents, the case manager oversees and coordinates a written individualized service plan (ISP) for each resident. The ISP specifies the necessary health care services, including any provided by a licensed home care agency. The case manager provides information and referral, coordinates with the providers chosen by the resident, and uses a formal mechanism to flag abrupt or progressive changes in behavior or appearance. [AGENCY NAME] employs a case manager who meets the on-site hours required for the number of ALR beds, and obtains DOH approval of the case manager where required for the adult home. The ISP content follows the ALR rules on service plans. Cross-reference: the full content requirements are in 10 NYCRR §1001.7, which counsel and the Administrator will confirm and incorporate before adoption.

definitions.definition: The qualified person designated by [AGENCY NAME] to coordinate resident evaluations, the ISP, referrals and communication with providers.
A written plan for each resident identifying his or her needs, strengths, preferences and the services that will be provided, by whom and how often.
Helping residents learn about and connect with community, health and social services.
A formal process for staff to report sudden or gradual changes in a resident's behavior or appearance to the case manager.

procedures: The Administrator designates the case manager in writing and, for the adult home, obtains DOH approval of the case manager before the person serves in the role. The Administrator may designate himself or herself as case manager if the home has fewer than 50 beds and he or she is qualified. The Administrator confirms this against the current DOH rules before doing so.

The Administrator sets the case manager's scheduled on-site hours to meet the minimum for the number of ALR beds: under 25 beds, at least 20 hours per week; 25 to 44 beds, 20 hours plus 1 hour for each bed over 24; 45 or more beds, at least 40 hours per week on site. The Administrator documents the calculation and updates it when the bed count changes.

The case manager records the actual on-site hours on a weekly time record, and the Administrator reviews it at least monthly. When a coverage gap occurs, the Administrator arranges a qualified substitute and notifies the DOH regional office within 3 business days if the case manager position is vacant (STF-01).
Before admission, the case manager completes the evaluation described in ARD-02 and meets with the resident to hear his or her preferences, goals, routines and choice of providers.

Within [number of days, recommended 14] days of admission, the case manager drafts the ISP with the resident, the representative if the resident agrees, the nurse or home care agency, and direct-care staff, and obtains the resident's signature or records why it was not signed.

The ISP identifies the resident's needs and strengths, the personal care and other services the home will provide, the health care services needed, and who provides them. It records any services from a licensed home care agency or other outside provider, hospice, or therapy, and lists the resident's chosen physician and other providers.

The case manager provides information and referral about community, social, financial and health resources, and helps the resident set up appointments, benefits and outside services as needed. Residents may use outside providers of their choice and choose their own health care providers.

The case manager coordinates with each provider the resident has chosen, including exchanging information (with the resident's consent), confirming orders and visit schedules, and updating the ISP when providers change.
The case manager gives direct-care staff a summary of each resident's ISP they need to do their work, in a location that protects privacy, and reviews changes with staff on each shift.

The case manager operates the change-flag mechanism: any staff member who notices an abrupt or progressive change in a resident's behavior or appearance, such as new confusion, weight change, withdrawal, bruising, or mood change, reports it the same shift using the [CHANGE REPORT FORM]. The case manager reviews each report within one business day, follows up with the nurse, physician or family as needed (HCS-04), and documents the outcome.
The case manager reviews and updates each ISP at least every 12 months with the reassessment (ARD-02), after any hospitalization, on a significant change in condition, and when the resident asks.
If the case manager finds a resident's needs have grown beyond what the home can lawfully serve, the case manager informs the Administrator immediately so that ARD-04 and ARD-05 are followed.
The Administrator reviews a sample of ISPs, change reports and case management hours every month and reports findings to the QA committee at least every six months (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Designates and obtains approval for the case manager, ensures required hours, reviews ISPs and audit results.
Writes and updates ISPs, coordinates providers, provides information and referral, and operates the change-flag mechanism.
Contribute health care needs and services to the ISP and report changes.
Follow the ISP, report abrupt or progressive changes, and give input on resident preferences.
Take part in planning, choose providers and approve the ISP.

documentation: Written designation of case manager and DOH approval, as applicable
Case manager qualification and hours calculation
Weekly case manager on-site time records
Pre-admission evaluation and individualized service plan with signature
ISP updates and review notes
Provider coordination and referral log
Change-flag reports and follow-up notes
QA audit reports

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with ALR, EALR and SNALR licensure; ALP participants
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps only residents whose needs it can lawfully and safely meet, and to set out what staff must do when a resident can no longer be retained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not accept or retain any person in a condition listed in 18 NYCRR 487.4(c). We re-check this at admission, at each annual medical evaluation, and on any change of condition. The 13 excluded conditions are: (1) a need for continual medical or nursing care; (2) a serious and persistent mental disability warranting placement in a Mental Hygiene Law facility; (3) a need for services that local providers cannot safely deliver; (4) danger to self or others; (5) repeated impairment of the well-being of others or of the orderly operation of the facility; (6) an unstable condition requiring continual skilled observation; (7) refusal or inability to comply with prescribed treatment, including medications, where a physician finds life-threatening danger; (8) chronically bedfast status; (9) chronic unmanaged urinary or bowel incontinence; (10) a dangerous communicable disease; (11) dependence on medical equipment unless all six conditions in 487.4(c)(11) are met; (12) aggressive or destructive alcohol or drug use; and (13) age under 18. Residents in the EALR may be retained under the aging-in-place rules of Public Health Law 4655 with the physician's report. EALR and SNALR residents who need 24-hour skilled nursing must be discharged unless all four conditions in 10 NYCRR 1001.10(m)(5) are met. Hospice may be provided only under the conditions in 1001.10(k)(4). When a resident cannot be retained, the Administrator will make and document persistent efforts at alternative placement.

definitions.definition: Care that must be provided around the clock by licensed medical or nursing staff and that the facility is not approved or staffed to deliver.
Retention of a resident whose needs have increased, permitted in an Enhanced Assisted Living Residence on the basis of a physician's report and the conditions in Public Health Law 4655.
A documented check of a resident's current condition against the excluded conditions in 18 NYCRR 487.4(c) and the service limits of the facility's license.
The NYS Department of Health regional office with jurisdiction over the facility.

procedures: At every pre-admission interview the Administrator and Case Manager screen the applicant against each of the 13 excluded conditions and record the result on the admission screening checklist (see ARD-01).

The Case Manager confirms that the medical evaluation (DSS-3122) was completed within 30 days before admission and is repeated at least every 12 months. Any evaluation that shows an excluded condition is sent to the Administrator the same day.
Do not admit an applicant who has an excluded condition. The Administrator documents the reason in the applicant file and helps the applicant and family find an appropriate setting.

For an applicant dependent on medical equipment, the Administrator checks each of the six conditions in 18 NYCRR 487.4(c)(11) in writing. If any condition is not met, the applicant is not admitted. If all are met, the file shows how each one is met.
The Case Manager performs a retention review at each annual reassessment (see ARD-02) and whenever staff report a change of condition (see HCS-04). The review is dated and signed.

Any staff member who observes signs of an excluded condition (for example, resident becomes bedfast, develops unmanaged incontinence, needs skilled observation, or is dangerous) reports it to the Case Manager or Administrator before the end of the shift.
On receiving a report, the Case Manager notifies the resident's physician and the resident's representative or next of kin and requests an updated medical evaluation if needed.

The Administrator, with the physician's input, decides whether the condition can be met under the current license, or under EALR/SNALR rules, or whether the resident can no longer be retained. The decision and reasons are written in the record.
For an EALR resident, the Administrator obtains the physician's report required for aging in place before retaining the resident beyond the usual limits. The report is filed in the resident record.

For an EALR or SNALR resident who needs 24-hour skilled nursing, the Administrator confirms in writing whether all four conditions in 10 NYCRR 1001.10(m)(5) are met. If any is not met, the resident is discharged using the process in ARD-05.
For a resident receiving hospice, the Administrator confirms that the conditions in 10 NYCRR 1001.10(k)(4) are met and records this. Coordination follows HCS-08.

If a resident cannot be retained, the Case Manager begins alternative placement efforts at once. Staff submit at least 5 applications to appropriate facilities and follow up by telephone every 2 weeks.
If any application is rejected, staff submit a new application within 5 working days of the rejection.
If the resident is not placed, the Administrator sends a written report on placement efforts to the regional office every 90 days until placement.
Every placement contact (facility, date, person spoken to, outcome) is logged on the Placement Efforts Log in the resident record.

Before a resident returns from a hospital or skilled nursing facility, the Administrator obtains the referral statement and confirms the resident still meets retention criteria. If not, the resident is not accepted back (see HCS-04).
The Administrator reports the number and type of retention-related discharges to the QA/QI Committee each quarter (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Makes final admission and retention decisions, confirms the equipment, aging-in-place and hospice conditions in writing, files the 90-day placement reports and keeps the retention review process current.
Performs retention reviews, tracks medical evaluation due dates, coordinates with physicians and families, and runs placement efforts.
Assesses clinical changes, advises on whether skilled nursing needs exceed what can be provided, and documents nursing findings.
Report observed changes in condition promptly to the Case Manager or Administrator.

documentation: Admission screening checklist showing review against each excluded condition
DSS-3122 medical evaluations (pre-admission and annual)
Written six-condition determination for medical equipment (487.4(c)(11))
Dated retention reviews
EALR physician's report
1001.10(m)(5) four-condition determination
Placement Efforts Log and copies of applications and rejections
90-day reports to the regional office with transmittal confirmation

policies.title: Involuntary Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with ALR, EALR and SNALR licensure; ALP participants
policies.purpose: To make sure any involuntary discharge, transfer or relocation of a resident follows the notice, court and advocacy requirements of 18 NYCRR 487.5(f) and protects the resident's rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not terminate a resident's residency or relocate a resident against their wishes except for a reason allowed by 18 NYCRR 487.5(f)(14), and only after giving the required notice and, when the resident objects, obtaining a court order. The facility gives at least 30 days' written notice on the DOH-prescribed form to the resident, the next of kin (if known) and any designated responsible party. Notice states the reason, the date and the resident's right to object. The notice is accompanied by the list of free legal and advocacy services, and a copy is filed with the regional office within 5 days of service. A resident who objects may remain while the facility commences a court proceeding. A shorter-notice transfer is allowed only for conditions requiring continual skilled care and for imminent risk of death or serious harm, as described in 487.5(f)(7)-(11). Residents may always object to a termination (487.5(a)(3)(xix)).

definitions.definition: Termination of residency or transfer of a resident initiated by the facility without the resident's agreement.
The Department of Health form that must be used for a termination notice; no substitute letter may be used.
A person named by the resident or by law to receive notices or act on the resident's behalf.

definitions.term: Free legal and advocacy services list
definitions.definition: The list of legal and advocacy organizations, including the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, that must accompany any termination notice.

procedures: A staff member who believes a resident may need to be discharged tells the Administrator at once. The Administrator opens a discharge review file.

The Administrator confirms in writing that the proposed reason is permitted under 18 NYCRR 487.5(f)(14), for example continual medical or nursing care the facility is not licensed to provide. The Administrator reviews the full subdivision each time and does not rely on memory or a summary. If there is any doubt, the Administrator consults legal counsel and the regional office before proceeding.

Before notice is given, the Case Manager meets with the resident and representative to discuss concerns, offer services that may resolve the problem, and document the outcome. If the reason is a change in condition, the Case Manager obtains an updated physician's evaluation (see ARD-04).
The Administrator completes the DOH-prescribed termination notice form, stating the specific reason, the discharge date (at least 30 days after service) and the resident's right to object.
Attach the current list of free legal and advocacy services, including Ombudsman contact information (see RR-03).

Serve the notice in writing on the resident, the next of kin (if known) and any designated responsible party. Use hand delivery or another method that gives proof of delivery. Staff read or explain the notice to the resident in a language and manner they understand (see RR-08).
Within 5 days of service, send a copy of the notice to the regional office. Record the date and method of filing.
Tell the resident that they may object and stay in the facility while the operator commences a court proceeding. Record the objection if one is made.

If the resident objects, the Administrator refers the matter to legal counsel for a court proceeding. The resident is not discharged unless and until the court approves, consistent with 487.5(d)(6)(xvi)(c).

Begin discharge planning at once. The Case Manager coordinates with the resident, family, physician and receiving provider to identify a safe, appropriate destination and carries out the placement steps in ARD-04.

For a shorter-notice transfer, the Administrator and the physician (or RN for EALR/SNALR) document that the resident has a condition requiring continual skilled care, or that there is an imminent risk of death or serious harm. Staff seek police assistance where possible and appropriate. Use the transfer steps in HCS-04.
If the resident is transferred without prior notice, hand-deliver the termination notice at the new location and document the delivery (487.5(f)(7)-(11)).
If the basis for a shorter-notice transfer no longer exists, readmit the resident when they are eligible and a bed is available, subject to retention criteria in ARD-04.

At discharge, return the resident's funds and personal property with a signed receipt (see RR-05), send medications per physician or pharmacy direction (see HCS-01), and send records and information to the receiving provider as required.
Calculate and pay any refund due under the admission agreement (see RR-04).
The Administrator closes the review file with all notices, proofs of service, court papers and the final disposition, and reports the case to the QA/QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether a lawful ground exists, signs and serves the DOH notice form, files the regional office copy within 5 days, and works with legal counsel on court proceedings.
Meets with the resident and family, coordinates discharge planning, obtains updated evaluations, and maintains the discharge file.
Authorizes legal action and ensures that discharges are not used for retaliation or convenience (see GOV-01).
Documents clinical grounds for any shorter-notice transfer.

documentation: Discharge review file with written basis under 487.5(f)(14)
Completed DOH-prescribed termination notice and proof of service on each recipient
List of free legal and advocacy services as given
Copy of notice filed with the regional office and date of filing
Resident's objection and any court papers and orders
Medical documentation for shorter-notice transfer
Discharge plan, placement log and receiving-provider communications
Receipts for funds, property and records released

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with ALR, EALR and SNALR licensure; ALP participants
policies.purpose: To make sure medications at [AGENCY NAME] are stored securely, handled safely, tracked accurately and disposed of properly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps all resident medications in secure storage at all times, meaning locked storage that cannot be entered or removed from at will. The only exception is a resident who must carry a medication for frequent or emergency use (18 NYCRR 487.7(f)(11)(i)-(ii)). The facility will not retain controlled substance prescriptions unless it first holds a class 3a Institutional Dispenser, Limited license from DOH. External-use drugs are stored apart from internal and injectable drugs. Medications are not kept in a food refrigerator unless in a separate locked compartment. Staff do not pour medications from one container to another, except for temporary absences. Only a physician or pharmacist may change label directions. As an ALR, [AGENCY NAME] maintains written medication policies and procedures that meet 487.7(f) and the ALR requirements of 10 NYCRR 1001.10(l), follow applicable state controlled-substance and professional practice rules, and follow current DOH guidance. A medication assistance record is kept for every resident.

definitions.definition: A locked cabinet, cart, drawer or room that residents and unauthorized persons cannot open or remove medications from at will.
A resident-specific record of diagnoses, all prescription and OTC medications, indication, special directions, allergies and a photo or electronic identifier.
A DOH license required before the facility may retain controlled substance prescriptions.
A medication ordered 'as needed' that is given only when the resident's symptoms or behaviors meet the physician's stated criteria.

procedures: Designate one locked medication storage area (room, cabinet or cart) for each unit. The Administrator keeps a list of who holds keys or codes and reviews it monthly.
Keep the storage area locked whenever it is not in use. Staff never leave keys, codes or open carts unattended.

A resident may keep medication in their room only when the physician has ordered or approved it for frequent or emergency use, such as an inhaler or nitroglycerin. The Case Manager records this in the ISP and checks that the resident can keep it safe (see ARD-03).

Do not retain a resident's controlled substance prescription unless the facility holds the class 3a Institutional Dispenser, Limited license. If it is not held, the resident or representative must arrange another lawful way of handling the prescription.
Store external-use drugs (creams, drops, patches, ointments) on a separate shelf or in a separate container from oral and injectable drugs.

If refrigeration is needed, use a dedicated medication refrigerator or a separate locked compartment in another refrigerator. Do not store medication in an unlocked food refrigerator. Log the temperature daily, with a range set by the pharmacy.

Keep each medication in its original pharmacy-labeled container. Staff do not pour or transfer medications between containers. For a temporary absence, a staff member or pharmacist prepares a labeled supply in accordance with pharmacy instructions and records the quantity sent.
Staff never alter, relabel or cross out a label. Direction changes come only from a physician or pharmacist, and staff update the medication assistance record the same day.

For each resident, the Case Manager or RN creates and keeps a medication assistance record that lists diagnoses, all prescription and OTC medications, the reason for each, special directions, allergies, and a photo or electronic identifier. The record is updated within one business day of any change (see HCS-02).

On receipt of medications from the pharmacy or family, two staff members check the delivery against the orders, record the count for controlled substances, and note any discrepancy to the Administrator or RN the same day.
Count controlled substances (where held) at every shift change with two staff signatures, and report any discrepancy to the Administrator immediately.
Check storage areas weekly for expired, discontinued or unlabeled medications. Remove them from active stock and place them in a locked 'for disposal' container.

Dispose of discontinued, expired or deceased residents' medications as set out in the facility's written medication disposal procedure, which follows DOH guidance and applicable law. The Administrator or RN and a second staff witness document the resident's name, drug, strength, quantity, date and method of disposal, and both sign. Controlled substances are disposed of only by a method allowed by law, with a witness and record.
Return a resident's medications to the resident or representative on discharge only on physician or pharmacist direction, with a signed receipt.
The Administrator or RN reviews storage, counts, medication assistance records and disposal logs monthly and reports findings to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05).
Medication errors, missing medication and loss or theft are reported on an incident report the same shift (see SAF-02).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains written medication policies, holds required licenses, controls keys and codes, and reviews medication logs monthly.
Maintains medication assistance records, trains staff on storage and handling, and reviews disposal logs.
Keep storage locked, follow storage and handling rules, and record all counts and disposals.
Provides labeling, advice on storage and disposal, and periodic review as arranged by the facility.

documentation: Medication assistance record for each resident
Key and code list for medication storage
Refrigerator temperature log
Controlled substance receipt and count log (if licensed)
Copy of class 3a Institutional Dispenser, Limited license (if held)
Medication disposal log with witness signatures
Monthly medication storage review
Incident reports for errors, loss or theft

policies.title: Assistance with Self-Administration of Medication and Staff Authorization Limits
policies.applies_to: Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with ALR, EALR and SNALR licensure; ALP participants
policies.purpose: To define when residents may manage their own medications, what staff may and may not do to help, and how physician orders are followed.
policies.policy: A resident may self-administer medication only if the physician has attested in writing to the resident's capability and the resident keeps [AGENCY NAME] informed of all medications taken (18 NYCRR 487.7(f)(1)-(2)). For residents who need help, trained staff give the proper dose at the designated time, and observe and record that it is taken. The person assisting must remove or prepare the dose. Staff may not administer injectables. A licensed professional may give an injectable only if providers customarily train a patient or family to give it, and insulin syringes may be prefilled only by a nurse (487.7(f)(6)-(7)). Staff never change a dose or schedule without prior written physician authorization. In an emergency, a phone order must be confirmed in writing within 7 days. PRN medications follow 10 NYCRR 1001.10(l)(4)-(7). EALR advanced home health aides may perform advanced tasks only under 10 NYCRR 1001.11(r).

definitions.definition: A resident takes medication without staff help, after a physician's written attestation of capability.
Staff provide the correct dose at the right time, observe that the resident takes it, and record it. The staff member removes or prepares the dose.
An aide on the home care worker registry who, under RN direction, may perform tasks beyond basic home health aide tasks in an EALR or SNALR.
An emergency order from a physician by phone, which must be confirmed in writing within 7 days.

procedures: Before admission and at each annual evaluation, the Case Manager reviews the physician's medical evaluation for a written statement on whether the resident can self-administer. If there is no statement, the resident is treated as needing assistance until one is obtained.

For self-administering residents, the Case Manager keeps the physician's attestation on file, asks the resident to report every medication they take (including OTC and new prescriptions), and records the list in the medication assistance record (see HCS-01). The Case Manager reviews it at least monthly and whenever the resident returns from a hospital.
For residents who need help, only staff who have completed medication assistance training and been found competent (see STF-04) may assist. The Administrator keeps a current list of authorized staff.
At each medication pass, the assisting staff member washes hands, checks the resident's identity against the photo or electronic identifier, and checks the order, the medication label and the record.

The staff member removes or prepares the dose, hands it to the resident, observes that it is taken, and records it right away on the medication assistance record. The staff member never prepares doses ahead of time for another person to give.

Staff do not administer any injectable medication. If a resident requires an injectable, only a licensed professional may give it, and only where providers customarily train patients or families to give that drug. Insulin syringes may be prefilled only by a nurse. Otherwise the resident self-injects or the nurse gives it. If neither is possible, the Administrator reviews retention under ARD-04.

If a resident refuses a medication, or is unable to take it, the staff member records the refusal or inability on the record and notifies the prescriber, and the primary physician if different, on the same day. The call and response are documented.

Staff never change a dose or schedule on their own. A change requires prior written physician authorization. In an emergency, staff may act on a telephone order, which the RN or Case Manager writes down, reads back, and obtains written confirmation of within 7 days. Follow up daily until received.
If a physician other than the primary physician prescribes or discontinues a drug, the Case Manager notifies the primary physician within 1 business day and documents it.

PRN orders must state the behaviors or symptoms that warrant use. If the physician has not stated that the resident can identify the need for the PRN, staff may not assist without observing the resident or consulting licensed nursing or medical staff first, and they document the consultation. This applies to OTC PRN products too.
PRN medication for a resident with dementia is used only when the physician has found there is no alternative. The record shows the physician's finding.

For EALR advanced home health aides, the Administrator verifies registry status, 18 hours of annual in-service, and direct RN supervision with an RN visit at least every 2 weeks, before the aide performs any advanced task. Before assigning an advanced task, the RN completes a nursing assessment and medication review and gives written patient-specific instructions (see HCS-03).
Staff report any medication error, near-miss or adverse reaction to the RN or Case Manager immediately and complete an incident report during the same shift (see SAF-02).
The Case Manager or RN audits a sample of medication assistance records monthly and retrains staff as needed. Results go to the QA/QI Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps the authorized staff list, enforces the ban on injectables by unlicensed staff, and ensures competency before staff assist.
Reviews attestations and orders, takes and confirms telephone orders, supervises advanced home health aides and audits records.
Prepare and hand over doses, observe, record, report refusals and errors, and never alter doses or schedules.
Provides written attestations, orders, PRN parameters and written confirmation of phone orders.
