The Administrator will post evacuation procedures and routes on every floor and in each wing, and will keep emergency contact numbers and procedures in a binder at the staff station, available to all supervisory staff.

The Administrator will identify residents who need help to evacuate, such as those with mobility impairment, cognitive impairment or oxygen, and will keep a current list with each resident's needs for use during an emergency (see RR-08 and ARD-03).

The Administrator will make written arrangements with community resources, including a receiving facility or alternate site, transportation, the local emergency manager, pharmacy and utility providers, and will keep their contact details current.

Within [NUMBER] days of opening and on any change in staff, the Administrator will confirm that [AGENCY NAME] has an HPN account, designate HPN coordinators and users, and enter a 24/7 emergency contact in the HPN directory.

The Administrator or HPN coordinator will update the HPN directory whenever contacts change, and in any event at least monthly. The HPN coordinator will record the date of each monthly review. The Administrator will review the HPN coverage policy every year.

The shift emergency designee will activate the plan when an emergency occurs, will call 911 where life safety is threatened, and will notify the Administrator immediately. Staff will account for every resident using the census (see SAF-09).

If service must continue with reduced personnel, the Administrator will use the call list, adjust assignments to protect residents with the highest needs, and request staff from [BACKUP STAFFING SOURCE].

The Administrator will notify DOH by the next business day of any circumstance requiring implementation of the plan, including a fire, work stoppage, loss of a fire system, no hot water, or interruption of essential services. The Administrator will complete an Incident Report where required (see SAF-02).
After each activation or drill, the Administrator will hold a debriefing with staff to review performance, record problems and corrective actions, and revise the plan as needed.
The Administrator will report plan activations, debriefing outcomes and HPN status to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Write, maintain and submit the plan, train staff, maintain HPN, notify DOH and lead the post-event review.
Run the evacuation or disaster plan on the shift and account for all residents.
Maintain HPN accounts, the 24/7 contact and the monthly directory update.
Know the plan and their role, and follow directions during an emergency.
Approves the plan and any material changes.

documentation: DOH-approved written disaster and emergency plan with approval date
Training records for each employee and volunteer
Posted evacuation procedures and floor plans
List of residents needing evacuation assistance
HPN coordinator and user designation, 24/7 contact and monthly directory update log
Debriefing reports after each drill or activation
DOH notifications and Incident Reports
Agreements with community resources and receiving sites

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, supervisors, the Administrator and residents in the adult home / enriched housing program, ALR, EALR, SNALR and ALP
policies.purpose: To protect residents from fire by maintaining required fire protection systems, training all staff in rapid evacuation, and conducting and recording fire drills on the schedule DOH requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] conducts fire drills for staff and volunteers every month, at varied times of day and night, with full and partial evacuation and simulated fire conditions. At least one drill in each calendar quarter includes residents, and at least one drill every 12 months is a total evacuation. At least once a year, the Administrator arranges for local fire authorities, a certified service agency or DOH to observe a resident drill. The Administrator records the date, time, description, number of residents, and the signatures of the staff and volunteers who took part, and keeps the records. All employees are trained in rapid evacuation. Buildings with 25 or more beds have sprinklers throughout and at least one fire protection system connected to the local fire department. The Administrator notifies DOH by the next business day of a fire or loss of a fire system.

definitions.definition: A drill in which all residents are moved out of the building to a safe place.
A drill in which residents in part of the building, such as a wing or floor, are moved to a safe area.
A drill in which every resident leaves the building, required at least once every 12 months.
An outside organization qualified to observe fire drills and inspect fire protection systems.
The building's alarm, detection and sprinkler systems.

procedures: The Administrator will confirm that the building has sprinklers throughout if it has 25 or more beds, and at least one fire protection system connected to the local fire department. The Administrator will keep the inspection and test records.

The Administrator will have the fire alarm, detection, sprinkler and extinguishing equipment inspected and tested on the schedule set by the local fire authority and the manufacturer, and will correct any defect immediately.

If any fire protection system is out of service, the Administrator will notify the DOH regional office by the next business day, will start a fire watch with extra staff until it is restored, and will complete an Incident Report (see SAF-02).

The Administrator will schedule a staff and volunteer fire drill every month, and will vary the day, shift and time so that day and night staff are covered. Each year the drills will include full and partial evacuation and simulated fire conditions.

At least once in every calendar quarter, the Administrator will include residents in the drill. Staff will tell residents beforehand how to take part safely and will help residents who need assistance, including those with mobility or cognitive impairment.
At least once every 12 months, the drill will be a total evacuation of the building.

At least once a year, the Administrator will arrange for the local fire authorities, a certified service agency or DOH to observe a resident drill. The Administrator will keep the written report or observer's confirmation.

At each drill, the shift emergency designee will direct the evacuation, account for every resident with the census, and note any problem such as blocked exits, slow response, or a resident who did not hear the alarm.

The staff and volunteers who take part will sign the drill record. The Administrator will record the date, time, description, number of residents, and signatures of the staff and volunteers who took part, and will keep the drill records on file.
After every drill, the Administrator will hold a short debriefing, record corrective actions, and complete any repairs or retraining within [NUMBER] days.

The Administrator will train all employees in rapid evacuation at orientation, before they work alone, and again at least annually, using the building layout, alarm locations, exits and extinguisher use (see STF-03).

The Administrator will post evacuation routes on every floor and in each wing, and will keep exits, corridors and stairs clear at all times. Staff will report any blocked exit immediately and clear it.

In an actual fire, staff will rescue anyone in immediate danger, activate the alarm, call 911, close doors, evacuate residents following the plan, and account for everyone with the census (see SAF-05 and SAF-09).
After a fire, the Administrator will notify DOH by the next business day, complete the Incident Report, notify the residents' representatives, and arrange for temporary housing if needed.
The Administrator will report drill results, equipment problems and corrective actions to the QA/QI Committee (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Schedule and record drills, arrange annual outside observation, keep systems inspected, notify DOH, and train staff.
Direct evacuations and drills on the shift and account for every resident.
Keep exits clear and fire equipment in working order, and report defects.
Take part in drills, know evacuation routes and help residents evacuate.

documentation: Fire drill records with date, time, description, number of residents and staff and volunteer signatures
Record of quarterly resident drills and annual total evacuation
Annual outside observer report or confirmation
Inspection and test records for alarm, detection and sprinkler systems
Evidence of connection to the local fire department
Debriefing notes and corrective action records
Staff evacuation training records
DOH notifications and Incident Reports for fires or system loss

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control, Bloodborne Pathogens and Exposure Management
policies.applies_to: All residents, employees, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] (Adult Home / Enriched Housing Program with Assisted Living Residence, EALR, SNALR and ALP, as licensed)
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents and staff, to prevent occupational exposure to blood and other significant-risk body substances, and to ensure that any exposure is reported, evaluated, treated and kept confidential as required by New York State and OSHA.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] implements and enforces a written infection control and bloodborne pathogen exposure prevention program. The program includes protective barriers, safe handling of sharps and contaminated equipment, personal protective equipment (PPE), training at hire and at least annually, and monitoring of staff compliance. Any exposure to a significant-risk body substance is reported to a designated person, evaluated, and followed up medically, with the source individual assessed and counseled as appropriate. Staff do not work while they have a communicable disease. Residents with a communicable disease that endangers others are not retained. HIV-related information is disclosed only with the person's express written consent or a court order. The Quality Improvement Committee reviews infection control performance standards as part of the quality assurance plan.

definitions.definition: Blood and other body substances capable of transmitting bloodborne or other infectious disease, as defined in the facility's exposure control plan.
A needlestick, cut, splash or other contact of blood or body substances with broken skin, mucous membranes or eyes, or other contact identified in the exposure control plan.
The person whose blood or body substances were involved in an exposure.
The staff member appointed by the Administrator to receive exposure reports and coordinate follow-up: [INFECTION CONTROL DESIGNEE NAME/TITLE].
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.

procedures: The Administrator appoints an infection control designee in writing and posts the designee's name and [PHONE] at each staff station and in the staff handbook.

The designee maintains a written Exposure Control Plan that lists job tasks with exposure risk, protective barriers, sharps handling, handling of contaminated laundry, equipment and waste, PPE, and the post-exposure procedure. The Plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever tasks or equipment change.

Before any staff member performs resident care, the facility trains the employee on the Exposure Control Plan, standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE use and the exposure reporting steps. This is part of orientation. The employee signs an attendance record.
All staff repeat the training at least annually. Resident aides' annual in-service hours include infection control and bloodborne pathogen content (see STF-04).

The facility supplies gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection, hand hygiene supplies, puncture-resistant sharps containers and spill kits at no cost to staff, and the housekeeping and nursing leads check stock weekly.

Staff use standard precautions with every resident. They wash hands before and after resident contact, wear gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin or contaminated items, and place used sharps immediately in sharps containers. Needles are not recapped by hand.
Housekeeping and laundry staff follow written procedures for cleaning and disinfecting blood or body fluid spills, handling soiled linen, and disposing of regulated waste (see DL-03).

When a staff member is exposed, the staff member immediately washes the area with soap and water or flushes the eyes or mucous membranes, and reports the exposure to the designated person or the supervisor on duty right away, on every shift.

The designated person completes an Exposure Incident Report the same day. It records who was exposed, the date and time, the circumstances, the body substance and the PPE in use. The designated person arranges for the exposed person to be evaluated by a physician or clinic as soon as possible, ideally within the same day, so that any recommended post-exposure treatment can be started promptly.

The designated person identifies the source individual and has the resident's physician or other qualified clinician assess the source and provide counseling. Testing of the source individual is done only in accordance with New York law and with the required consent. The designated person does not disclose HIV-related information without express written consent of the person or a court order (see RR-07).

The exposed individual is offered medical follow-up, counseling and any recommended prophylaxis. The results of the evaluation are given to the exposed individual in accordance with law. Medical information is kept in a confidential file separate from the personnel file.

The Administrator reviews each exposure within 7 days to determine whether a device, practice or training gap contributed, takes corrective action, and records it. The event is also handled under SAF-02 if it meets incident report criteria.

A resident who shows signs of a communicable disease is promptly assessed by nursing staff or arranged for evaluation by the resident's physician. The facility notifies the physician, implements isolation or precautions as ordered, and may use a sick bay or isolation area within the facility's certified capacity. Required public health reports are made to the local health department.

If a resident has a communicable disease that endangers others and the facility cannot protect other residents, the Administrator follows ARD-04 and ARD-05 on retention limits and discharge, including persistent efforts to find an alternative placement.

Staff with symptoms of a communicable disease (such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea or a rash) report to the supervisor and do not work until cleared. Return-to-work is documented. Annual employee health statements and TB assessments are kept as described in STF-05.

For EALR and SNALR direct-care staff, the facility keeps immunization records for rubella and measles, unless the employee has a documented exemption, and keeps TB screening records in the personnel file.

The designee reports infection control data (infections, outbreaks, exposures, hand hygiene and PPE audits) to the Quality Improvement Committee at least every six months, and infection control performance standards are included in the quality assurance plan (see GOV-05).
Quarterly, the designee observes staff practice (hand hygiene, PPE, sharps handling) and records compliance. Staff who do not comply are retrained and the retraining is documented.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the designee, ensures resources and training, reviews exposures and keeps the program in force.
Maintains the Exposure Control Plan, receives exposure reports, coordinates follow-up, monitors compliance and reports to the Quality Improvement Committee.
Assess residents with signs of infection, notify physicians, implement precautions and assist in source-individual assessment.
Use standard precautions and PPE, handle sharps safely, report exposures and illness immediately, and complete required training.
Clean, disinfect and dispose of contaminated materials according to procedure.

documentation: Written Exposure Control Plan with annual review dates
Training rosters and curriculum for orientation and annual training
Exposure Incident Reports and follow-up records (confidential medical file)
Compliance monitoring and audit records
Employee health statements, TB assessments and immunization records
Quality Improvement Committee minutes including infection control reports
Isolation and communicable disease notifications

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: All residents, visitors, volunteers and staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set clear facility rules for smoking, visiting and animals that protect resident health and safety while respecting residents' rights to private communication, community life and a personalized living space.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] sets written rules on smoking, visiting hours and pets that comply with the New York State Clean Indoor Air Act, local fire codes and the resident rights statement. The facility gives these rules, including its rules on resident activities, office hours and visiting hours, to every applicant at or before the admission interview. Residents may communicate privately with anyone of their choice and may not be denied community life. Rules are applied equally and are limited to what is needed for safety and orderly operation. Residents may decorate their rooms in compliance with fire and safety codes.

definitions.definition: Any person who is not a resident or employee and is on the premises to see a resident or conduct business.
An outdoor area approved by the Administrator, located in compliance with the Clean Indoor Air Act and local fire code, away from building entrances and air intakes.
A dog or other animal individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, which is allowed under applicable disability law.
An animal that the facility keeps on the premises for the benefit of residents under this policy.

procedures: The Administrator, with the Quality Improvement Committee and the Resident Council, adopts written facility rules on smoking, visiting and animals. The Administrator reviews the rules at least annually and when laws or fire codes change.

Smoking, including e-cigarettes and vaping, is prohibited inside the building, in resident rooms and in vehicles used for transportation. The Administrator designates an outdoor smoking area that complies with the Clean Indoor Air Act and the local fire marshal's requirements, and posts signs.

Smoking materials are not left unattended. The facility provides non-combustible receptacles and a supervised location. Staff report to the Administrator any smoking violation or smoking-related fire hazard the same shift.

The Case Manager asks each applicant about smoking. If a resident smokes, the resident's ISP records any need for supervision or safety measures (for example, cognitive impairment, oxygen use or burn risk), and the facility offers cessation resources through the resident's physician.
No smoking or open flames are permitted near oxygen. Staff post oxygen signs and keep the area clear. The facility handles resident oxygen safely (see SAF-06).

At or before the admission interview, the Administrator or Case Manager gives the applicant a written copy of the facility rules covering resident activities, office hours and visiting hours, and documents that the applicant received them (see ARD-01 and RR-04).

Visiting hours are [VISITING HOURS], and the facility posts them at the main entrance. The facility does not use visiting hours to restrict a resident's right to see people privately. Reasonable arrangements are made for visitors at other times, especially for family, clergy, the Ombudsman, legal or advocacy representatives, and during a resident's serious illness.

The front desk or staff on duty asks visitors to sign in and out in the visitor log, directs them to the resident, and tells them about infection control or emergency instructions as needed. Visitors cannot be required to give personal information beyond what is needed for safety.
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman, the Department of Health and legal and advocacy representatives are granted access to residents as described in RR-03 and are not limited by visiting hours.

Residents may meet visitors in their rooms, common areas or outdoors. The facility provides a private space for meetings and telephone calls. Staff do not read or open a resident's mail or listen to their calls.

If a visitor is disruptive, threatens anyone, appears to be ill with a communicable disease or violates fire or safety rules, the staff on duty asks the visitor to leave and calls the Administrator or on-call administrator. If a visitor poses an immediate threat, staff call 911. The Administrator records the incident and, when needed, restricts a visitor only after consulting the resident and documenting the reason. A resident's choices are respected whenever possible.

Service animals are permitted in all areas open to residents. The facility asks only the two questions allowed by law: whether the animal is required because of a disability and what task it performs. It does not require documentation or fees.

Visiting pets are permitted if the owner provides proof of current rabies vaccination, the animal is leashed or contained, and the visit does not disturb other residents. The Administrator may restrict animals in food preparation areas, during an outbreak, or if an animal is unsafe.

Resident-owned pets and facility pets are permitted only if the Administrator has approved them in writing based on [PET RULES: e.g., size, number, vaccination, cleaning, resident ability to care]. Residents who keep a pet remain responsible for its care, and the ISP documents any assistance needed. Facility pets are cared for by assigned staff, and the facility respects residents with allergies or fears.

Residents may decorate their rooms with personal furnishings and belongings that comply with fire and safety codes. Staff do not allow space heaters, candles, extension cord misuse or other fire hazards. The facility explains the restriction and offers a safe alternative.
Complaints about smoking, visitors or animals are handled through RR-02. The Administrator reviews complaints and incidents at least quarterly and reports trends to the Quality Improvement Committee.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and enforces the rules, designates the smoking area, approves animals, handles disputes and ensures rules respect resident rights.
Reviews rules with applicants and residents, identifies smoking or pet safety needs in the ISP and documents receipt of rules.
Enforce the rules fairly, keep the visitor log, report hazards and violations and call for help as needed.
Follow the posted rules, smoke only in the designated area, and care for any approved animal.

documentation: Written smoking, visitor and pet rules with review dates
Signed acknowledgment of rules given at or before the admission interview
Visitor log
Pet approvals, vaccination proof and care plans
Incident records related to smoking, visitors or animals
ISP entries on smoking or pet-related safety needs
Resident Council minutes showing rules were reviewed

policies.title: Resident Supervision, Daily Census and Call System Monitoring
policies.applies_to: All residents and all direct-care, supervisory and on-duty staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive continuous on-site supervision, that staff know where residents are and notice changes, that emergency calls are answered, and that minimum supervision staffing is met 24 hours a day.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides 24-hour on-site supervision of residents. Supervision includes knowing residents' general whereabouts, recording the daily census on the Department of Health form, monitoring for changes in behavior or appearance, guiding residents in basic activities of daily living, watching grounds and activities, monitoring emergency call systems, responding to emergencies, conducting evacuations and drills, implementing the disaster plan and investigating incidents. The facility has at least the minimum number of staff on duty and on site at all times: 1 for a census of 1 to 40, 2 for 41 to 80, 3 for 81 to 150, 4 for 151 to 200, and 1 more for each additional 60 residents. At least one person qualified in first aid is on duty and on site at all times. For the Assisted Living Residence, the facility provides 24-hour on-site monitoring with the ability to respond to urgent needs and to identify abrupt or progressive changes in a resident's condition.

definitions.definition: The facility's responsibility for general oversight of residents' safety and wellbeing, including whereabouts, changes in condition and emergency response. It is not constant one-to-one observation.
The count of residents in the facility each day, recorded on the Department of Health census form.
Staff physically in the facility and available to residents, not on call and not off-site.
The resident call or alarm system required in the facility's environmental standards, which allows residents to summon staff.
A staff member with current first aid training documented in the personnel file.

procedures: The Administrator sets the staffing schedule for each shift so that the number of staff on duty and on site meets or exceeds the minimum for the current census (1 for 1-40, 2 for 41-80, 3 for 81-150, 4 for 151-200, and 1 more per additional 60). The schedule shows names, shifts and the person in charge, and is kept for 12 months (see STF-01).

Before each shift ends, the outgoing supervisor confirms that the incoming shift has the required number of staff on site. If the minimum cannot be met, the supervisor calls the Administrator or on-call administrator immediately, calls in replacement staff, and does not leave the facility below the minimum. The Administrator documents the cause and the remedy.

The Administrator ensures that at least one first-aid-qualified staff member is on every shift. The shift schedule identifies that person, and first aid certificates are tracked and renewed before they expire (see STF-03).

At [CENSUS TIMES, e.g., 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m.] daily, the supervisor on duty counts residents, accounts for those who are out, in the hospital or on leave, and records the census on the Department of Health form. The supervisor signs and dates it.
Staff track residents who sign out of the facility. The sign-out log shows the expected return time. Staff follow SAF-03 when a resident is not back by the expected time or cannot be located.

Staff keep general knowledge of where each resident is. At a minimum, they do a documented check of common areas, grounds and activities each [ROUND INTERVAL, e.g., 2 hours] and check on residents named in the ISP for more frequent monitoring, such as those at high fall risk or with dementia (see HCS-05, HCS-06).
Overnight, staff make documented rounds at least every [NIGHT ROUND INTERVAL], check exits, and record anything unusual. They respond to calls without delay.

Staff observe residents for changes in behavior, mood, appearance, appetite, mobility or health. They report to the supervisor during the shift, and the supervisor notifies the Case Manager, nurse or physician as appropriate and documents the observation (see HCS-04).
Staff guide residents in basic activities of daily living, remind them of meals, activities and appointments, and encourage participation, without taking over tasks the resident can safely do.

The call system is tested [WEEKLY] by maintenance staff, with results logged. A staff member is assigned to hear or see call signals at all times, including overnight. Defects are repaired promptly. If a part of the system fails, the Administrator arranges for interim measures such as extra rounds, and records it.

Staff answer a resident's call immediately. For an emergency they provide first aid, call 911 and notify the Administrator, the resident's physician and the emergency contact, and document the event under SAF-02 and HCS-04.

For an ALR, the nurse or Case Manager, depending on the resident's ISP, identifies residents who may experience abrupt or progressive changes. The supervisor makes sure staff know about the resident's baseline and the signs that require a call to the nurse or physician.

Staff conduct evacuation drills and are trained in the disaster plan as described in SAF-05 and SAF-06. During a drill or real event, the supervisor takes the census and confirms all residents are accounted for.

After any incident involving supervision, such as a fall, elopement, unnoticed change in condition or an unanswered call, the Administrator investigates within 24 hours, interviews staff, determines whether supervision was adequate and documents corrective action.

Each quarter, the Administrator compares schedules, census forms, call system logs and incident reports to look for staffing gaps or response problems, and reports to the Quality Improvement Committee (see GOV-05).
The Administrator reports key position vacancies and other staffing changes to the regional office as required in STF-01.

responsibilities.duty: Sets and verifies staffing that meets the supervision minimum, ensures first-aid coverage, investigates supervision failures and reports to the QI Committee.
Confirms staffing at shift change, records the daily census, assigns call monitoring and rounds, and calls for help or replacements.
Know residents' whereabouts, do rounds, answer calls, report changes in condition and give first aid.
Test and repair the call system and keep logs.
Identify residents needing more monitoring, include it in the ISP and respond to reported changes.

documentation: Staffing schedules (kept 12 months)
Daily census forms
Resident sign-out/sign-in log
Round and check logs
Call system test and repair logs
First aid certificates
Incident reports and investigations
Quality Improvement Committee minutes

policies.title: Food Service and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: All residents, food service staff, dietitian or dietetic technician, and care staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide safe, nutritious, appealing meals that respect each resident's health, allergies, culture, religion and preferences, with adequate staffing and qualified supervision.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides daily food service with qualified supervision and sufficient staff. Food service staffing is at least 2.0 hours per resident per week and never less than 35 hours per week. The facility has a food service manager. A qualified dietitian or dietetic technician supervises food service under a written agreement that states duties and the time to be spent. Food purchasing, storage, preparation and service follow State Sanitary Code food service requirements and local health codes. Menus take into account residents' health conditions, allergies, intolerances, religious and ethnic mandates and taste preferences. Records needed to plan prescribed diets, allergies and preferences are readily available to food service staff. Residents have access to reasonably available foods of their choice at any time. Meals are served in the dining room, except for short-term illness.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a physician or other authorized practitioner to treat a condition, such as diabetic, low-sodium, renal or texture-modified.
The employee responsible for day-to-day kitchen operation, staffing, sanitation, purchasing and menu implementation.
A qualified person who supervises food service and nutrition under a written agreement.
A record of a resident's diet order, allergies, intolerances, texture needs and preferences used by kitchen and dining staff.

procedures: The Administrator schedules food service staff to provide at least 2.0 hours per resident per week (resident census times 2.0) and never fewer than 35 hours per week. The Administrator reviews the schedule each month against the current census.
The Administrator designates a food service manager in writing, and the job description lists duties for menu planning, purchasing, sanitation, staff supervision and recordkeeping.

The Administrator signs a written agreement with a qualified dietitian or dietetic technician that states duties, such as menu approval, diet order review, sanitation and staff training, and the number of hours per [WEEK/MONTH] spent at the facility. The agreement is kept on file and reviewed annually.

The dietitian or dietetic technician approves menus, which are planned in advance, are nutritionally adequate and offer variety. The kitchen posts the weekly menu in a place visible to residents and keeps copies of menus as served, noting substitutions.

During the pre-admission interview and screening, the Case Manager asks about diet orders, allergies, intolerances, religious or ethnic food requirements and food preferences, and confirms the program can meet these needs. If it cannot, the Administrator explains this to the applicant under ARD-01.

The Case Manager or nurse enters dietary information from the medical evaluation and assessment into the resident's record and gives a diet card or equivalent to the kitchen within 24 hours of admission or a change in the diet order. Food service staff can see the information they need to plan diets, allergies and preferences, and confidentiality is protected.

When a physician or other authorized practitioner changes a diet order, the nurse or Case Manager updates the resident record, ISP and diet card the same day and notifies the kitchen and the dining staff. Staff do not change a therapeutic diet without an order.

The dietitian or dietetic technician reviews residents with therapeutic diets, weight loss, poor intake, chewing or swallowing difficulty and recommends changes to the Case Manager or physician. Staff weigh residents monthly as part of personal care and report significant weight changes (see HCS-04).

The kitchen follows written procedures for food purchasing from approved sources, storage temperatures, date labeling, cleaning, handwashing, cross-contamination prevention, allergen control, temperature logging and holding of hot and cold foods under the State Sanitary Code and local health code. The food service manager keeps temperature logs and cleaning records.
Food service staff complete food safety training at hire and at least annually. Staff with illness symptoms do not work in the kitchen (see SAF-07).

Meals are served in the dining room at regular times, with a mealtime schedule posted. Residents who need help receive it from trained staff who follow the ISP for texture, positioning and supervision. Staff do not leave residents who are at choking risk unattended while eating.

Residents who are ill for a short time may receive tray service in their rooms. Staff document it and notify the nurse or Case Manager if it lasts more than [NUMBER] days. Tray service is not used routinely for convenience.

The facility stocks snacks and beverages that are reasonably available and allows residents to get food at any time, including overnight. Residents on therapeutic diets receive appropriate alternatives.
The food service manager keeps purchase records, invoices and menus as program records. The records are retained as stated in REC-01.
The Administrator surveys residents on food quality at least quarterly, presents results at Resident Council and to the QI Committee, and records changes made. Complaints are handled under RR-02.
For emergencies, the kitchen keeps an emergency food and water supply, as set in the emergency plan (see SAF-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures staffing, qualified supervision, written agreement with the dietitian/technician and compliance with food safety rules.
Supervises kitchen staff, purchasing, sanitation, menus and diet cards, and keeps records.
Approves menus, reviews therapeutic diets and nutrition concerns and trains staff according to the written agreement.
Communicates diet orders, allergies and preferences to the kitchen, monitors weight and intake.
Serve meals as ordered, assist residents and report problems with eating or intake.

documentation: Food service staffing schedules and hours calculation
Written agreement with dietitian or dietetic technician
Weekly posted menus and menus as served
Food purchase records and invoices
Diet orders, diet cards and allergy lists
Temperature, cleaning and sanitation logs
Food safety training records
Resident food surveys and QI Committee minutes

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents, the Administrator, activities director or staff, and care staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide a varied activities program that meets residents' social, recreational, cultural and spiritual needs, encourages family and community ties, and respects each resident's choice about participating.
policies.policy: Activities is a required resident service at [AGENCY NAME]. The facility provides an activities program based on residents' interests and assessed needs. Personal care includes helping residents take part in activities. The monthly activities schedule is posted, and activity schedules are kept as program records. Residents are not required to participate in activities or in facility work. The facility has an activities director or staff as the regulations require for its size, and reports a vacancy in the activities director position to the regional office within 3 business days.

definitions.definition: Planned individual and group social, recreational, educational, physical, cultural and spiritual opportunities offered on-site and in the community.
The staff member responsible for planning and running the activities program. At 24 beds or fewer, the Administrator may fill this role. At 50 or more beds, qualified activities staff are required.
A vacancy in a position the regulations require to be filled, including the activities director, which must be reported to the regional office.

procedures: The Administrator assigns responsibility for activities. If the facility has 24 beds or fewer, the Administrator may serve as activities director. If the facility has 50 or more beds, the Administrator employs qualified activities staff and keeps their credentials and job description in the personnel file.

If the activities director position becomes vacant, the Administrator notifies the regional office in writing within 3 business days, keeps a copy, appoints an interim person and documents the date the position is filled (see STF-01).

During pre-admission screening, the Case Manager asks about the applicant's interests, hobbies, routines, faith, language and social and family ties, and confirms that the program can meet their social needs and foster family and community connections (see ARD-01).
As part of the annual assessment and ISP, the Case Manager records each resident's activity interests, abilities, barriers and any assistance needed to participate (see ARD-02, ARD-03).

The activities director plans a monthly calendar that includes a variety of daytime, evening and weekend options: social, physical, creative, educational, spiritual and community outings. It also includes options for residents who prefer small groups or one-to-one activities, residents with cognitive impairment and residents with mobility limits.
The activities director asks residents for ideas through the Resident Council, surveys and individual conversations, and documents how the feedback was used (see RR-02).

The facility posts the monthly activities schedule by the first day of each month in a place accessible to residents and gives copies on request. Changes are posted promptly. A copy of each month's schedule is kept as a program record.
Care staff remind and help residents get to activities, including residents who use wheelchairs or walkers, and offer encouragement. Staff do not force participation.
Residents are not required to take part in facility work, such as kitchen, laundry or maintenance tasks. A resident may volunteer only under STF-07.

The activities director maintains an attendance and participation record for each activity and notes residents who rarely take part. The Case Manager follows up with the resident to identify reasons and update the ISP.

The facility supports family and community ties by welcoming visitors, arranging family events, assisting residents in contacting loved ones and offering transportation for community events and religious services (see SAF-08, DL-04).
For residents in a SNALR memory care unit, activities are designed and led as described in HCS-05.
The activities director has the materials, space and budget needed. The Administrator reviews the budget at least annually.
Before outings, the activities director confirms safety, transportation, supervision, staff ratios and any resident-specific precautions, and records who attended.
The Quality Improvement Committee reviews activities participation and resident satisfaction at least every six months (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Provides qualified activities staff as required, reports vacancies, supports the budget and reviews outcomes.
Plan and run the program, post the monthly schedule, record attendance and gather resident input.
Records interests and needs in the assessment and ISP and follows up with residents who do not participate.
Help residents attend and take part in activities.

documentation: Monthly activities schedules (posted and retained)
Attendance and participation records
Activities director's job description and qualifications
Notices to the regional office of activities director vacancies
Resident interest information in assessments and ISPs
Resident Council minutes and satisfaction surveys
QI Committee minutes

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: All housekeeping, laundry, maintenance and supervisory staff, and all residents and areas of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep the building, residents' rooms, equipment and grounds clean, safe and in good repair, to meet environmental standards, and to maintain required records and notifications.
policies.policy: Housekeeping is a required service at [AGENCY NAME]. Housekeeping staffing is at least 1.0 hour per resident per week. The facility keeps the physical plant clean, sanitary and in good repair and meets the State environmental standards for bedroom size, toilet and bath ratios, call system and sprinklers. For an Assisted Living Residence, the facility also meets the additional ALR physical environment requirements. The facility keeps records of maintenance and environmental standards. The Administrator reports the loss of hot water or other essential services to the Department of Health by the next business day.

definitions.definition: The building, grounds, systems and equipment used by the facility.
Services needed for resident health and safety, such as hot water, heat, electricity, water, sewage, fire protection, call system and refrigeration.
Scheduled inspection, testing and servicing of systems and equipment.

The physical requirements for the facility, including minimum bedroom sizes (100 sq ft single, 160 sq ft double), at least 1 toilet per 6 and 1 bath per 10 residents, a call system, and sprinklers throughout buildings of 25 or more beds.

procedures: The Administrator schedules housekeeping staff to provide at least 1.0 hour per resident per week, calculated against the current census, and reviews the schedule monthly.

The Administrator appoints a housekeeping/maintenance lead. Written schedules assign cleaning of resident rooms, bathrooms, common areas, kitchen, dining areas, hallways and exterior, with the frequency for each. Rooms are cleaned at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly], and more often when soiled.
Housekeeping staff are trained at hire and annually on cleaning methods, chemical safety, safety data sheets, disinfection, standard precautions, spill cleanup and handling of waste (see SAF-07).
Chemicals are stored in locked or restricted areas away from food and medications, and labeled. Safety data sheets are available to staff.

Laundry is done on a schedule that gives each resident clean linens at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., weekly], and more often as needed. Staff separate soiled linens, use PPE, wash and dry them at temperatures set by the manufacturer and disinfectant guidance, and keep clean and soiled linen apart.

Residents' personal laundry is labeled, returned to the right resident and handled to avoid loss or damage. Residents who wish to do their own laundry are supported. Lost or damaged items are handled under RR-05.

The maintenance lead inspects the building at least [WEEKLY] using a checklist covering floors, lighting, handrails, grab bars, heating and cooling, hot water temperature, plumbing, doors, windows, exits, outdoor walkways and equipment, and records findings.

The facility checks that bedroom size, toilet and bath ratios, call system and sprinklers meet the State standards. The Administrator documents compliance, and any proposed change to rooms, use or capacity is reviewed with the Department of Health before it is made (see GOV-03).
The call system is tested on a schedule and repaired promptly (see SAF-09). Fire protection systems, including sprinklers, are inspected and maintained as stated in SAF-06.

Staff report any hazard or repair need to the maintenance lead using a work order. The lead assigns a priority, fixes urgent hazards immediately (or makes the area unusable and posts warnings), and records the date completed. Residents may also request repairs; requests are logged.
Hot water temperatures are checked and recorded at [FREQUENCY] at points of use for residents, kept at a safe range to prevent scalding and to provide adequate hot water.

If hot water or any other essential service is lost, the staff on duty immediately notifies the Administrator, who arranges for repair or alternative arrangements, protects residents' health and safety (for example, bottled water, heaters, relocation) and reports the loss to the Department of Health regional office by the next business day. The Administrator documents the event, the actions and the report (see REC-02, SAF-05).
Pest control services are provided on a regular schedule, and the facility records visits. Staff report signs of pests the same day.

Residents may decorate their rooms with their own furnishings if they comply with fire and safety codes (see SAF-08). Staff respect residents' privacy when cleaning, knock before entering and follow resident preferences when possible.
The Administrator reviews work orders, inspections and environmental concerns each quarter and reports to the QI Committee (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures staffing, budget, compliance with environmental standards and timely reporting of loss of essential services.
Schedules cleaning, laundry and inspections, handles work orders and keeps maintenance records.
Perform assigned duties safely and report hazards.
Report hazards, spills and maintenance needs promptly.

documentation: Housekeeping staffing schedules and hours calculation
Cleaning and laundry schedules and logs
Maintenance records, inspection checklists and work orders
Hot water and call system test logs
Pest control records
Records of environmental standards compliance
Reports of loss of essential services to the Department of Health
Training records for housekeeping staff

policies.title: Transportation
policies.applies_to: Adult Home, Enriched Housing Program, ALR/EALR/SNALR and ALP residents; all staff and volunteers who arrange or provide transportation
policies.purpose: To support residents' participation in community life outside the facility, to keep transportation safe, and to make sure any transportation charges are disclosed in advance and are at the resident's option.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each resident's right to take part in community life, including life outside the facility (18 NYCRR 487.5(a)(3)(xiv)). The facility helps residents arrange transportation for medical appointments, community activities and personal errands. Any charge for transportation beyond the basic rate is listed in the supplemental schedule of the admission agreement and is at the resident's option (487.5(d)(6)(v)-(vi)). Staff or volunteers who drive residents must hold a valid New York driver license and be covered by applicable insurance. Any accident on or off facility grounds that requires medical attention is reported on an Incident Report (487.7(d)(11)(vii)). [AGENCY NAME] does not restrict a resident's lawful travel outside the facility, except as the resident's own plan, physician or legal decision-maker directs.

definitions.definition: The standard charge in the admission agreement that covers the minimum services required by 18 NYCRR 487.7(a).
The part of the admission agreement that lists optional services and their charges, including transportation beyond the basic rate.
Transportation provided by facility staff or vehicles, or booked by the facility through a contracted carrier, for a resident.
The report completed for events listed in 487.7(d), including an accident that requires medical attention.

procedures: At admission, the case manager explains which transportation is included in the basic rate and which is optional and charged separately. The agreement's supplemental schedule must list every transportation charge (rate, unit, e.g., per trip or per mile, and any wait-time charge).

The resident (or legal representative) chooses in writing whether to use each optional transportation service. The resident's choice is recorded on or with the supplemental schedule. No resident is required to buy optional transportation as a condition of admission or continued residency.

The Administrator reviews the transportation charges and the supplemental schedule at least annually. Any change is given to residents in writing under the notice terms of the admission agreement (see RR-04).
Residents who can travel independently are not asked to account for their whereabouts beyond the sign-out practice described in SAF-09. Staff must respect the resident's right to come and go.

Staff post and maintain a list of transportation resources (public transit, paratransit, Medicaid transportation where the resident is eligible, volunteer drivers, taxi/livery) in a common area. The case manager helps residents book rides, including Medicaid non-emergency transportation for eligible residents.

For medical appointments, the case manager or designee schedules transportation, tells the resident what to bring (medication list, face sheet, insurance cards, advance directive copy where applicable), and sends relevant information to the provider.

Before a staff member or volunteer drives a resident in any vehicle, the Administrator verifies and documents a valid New York driver license, a driving record acceptable to the agency, and the insurance that covers the vehicle used. Vehicle ownership and insurance types are confirmed with the agency's counsel and insurer. Staff may not use an unverified personal vehicle to transport residents.

Drivers must have their license on them, use seat belts for all occupants, use child/adult safety devices where required, and may not use a handheld phone while driving. The driver confirms that each resident's wheelchair or mobility device is properly secured. Only vehicles equipped to secure wheelchairs may carry residents who use them.

Before departure, staff confirm each resident's destination, return time and any needs (oxygen, assistance with transfers, medications due during the outing) and take the resident's emergency contact information. Medication needed during the outing is handled under HCS-01 and HCS-02.
The facility keeps a transportation log for facility-provided trips: date, driver, vehicle, residents transported, destination, departure/return times, and any problems.

If a resident is injured in an accident, or becomes ill, on or off facility grounds, staff obtain emergency medical care first. Staff then notify the resident's physician and representative under HCS-04, and the Administrator or designee completes an Incident Report. Where an incident is reportable to the Justice Center, DOH or other agency, staff follow SAF-01, SAF-02 and REC-02.
A driver involved in a vehicle accident notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator notifies the insurer and, where required, law enforcement, and preserves vehicle and trip records.
If a resident does not return when expected from an outing, staff follow SAF-03 (Elopement and Missing Resident).
Complaints about transportation or charges are handled under RR-02. Any refund owed for a charged but unprovided trip is processed under RR-04.
The QA/QI Committee reviews transportation incidents, complaints and missed appointments at least annually (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Approves transportation charges and the supplemental schedule; verifies driver license and insurance; ensures Incident Reports are completed and reportable events are submitted.
Explains optional transportation at admission, books transportation, documents resident choice and coordinates appointments.
Maintain a valid license, follow vehicle safety rules, keep the trip log and report accidents or problems at once.
Confirm departures and returns and begin missing-resident steps if a resident does not return.

documentation: Admission agreement supplemental schedule showing transportation charges and the resident's optional-service election
Driver license, driving record check and insurance verification in the personnel or volunteer file
Transportation log
Incident Reports for accidents requiring medical attention
Resident transportation resource list and appointment records in the resident record

policies.title: Staffing Levels, Supervision and Key-Position Vacancies
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct-care, case management, housekeeping and food service staff, and nursing staff (EALR/SNALR); all programs
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] always has enough qualified staff on site to supervise and care for residents, to meet the New York minimum staffing levels, and to notify the DOH regional office of key vacancies on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] schedules at least the minimum 24-hour on-site supervision staff and the minimum weekly staff hours per resident required by 18 NYCRR 487.9. The 24-hour on-site minimum is: 1 staff member for a census of 1-40; 2 for 41-80; 3 for 81-150; 4 for 151-200; and 1 additional for each additional 60 residents. Weekly hours per resident are at least 3.75 for personal care (covering day and evening shifts), 1.0 for housekeeping, and 2.0 for food service, with a food service floor of 35 hours per week. Enriched housing programs also meet 18 NYCRR 488.9 (including case manager hours of 0.5 hour per resident per week and 6 hours per resident per week of combined personal care, housekeeping and food staff). ALR, EALR/SNALR and ALP programs meet the additional requirements of 10 NYCRR 1001.11 and 18 NYCRR 494.6. The facility keeps current written staffing schedules and retains past schedules for 12 months. The facility notifies the DOH regional office within 3 business days of a vacancy in a key position.

definitions.definition: The number of residents in the facility, used with the staffing table. [AGENCY NAME] uses the higher of the actual daily census or the staffing level for the facility's highest census in the week.
Staff physically present in the facility and responsible for resident supervision, who may not be counted as off-site or on-call.
Administrator, case manager, activities director, dietary consultant and health consultant (as listed in 487.9(a)(16)).

definitions.term: Staff hours per resident per week
definitions.definition: Total scheduled hours of the category (personal care, housekeeping, food service) divided by the weekly census. Hours worked by the Administrator or by case managers in other roles do not count unless the regulation allows.
The written schedule showing each staff member's name, position, shift and hours, with changes noted.

procedures: The Administrator uses the facility's census each week to calculate the required on-site staff count and the required weekly hours for personal care, housekeeping and food service. The calculation is kept with the schedule.

The Administrator (or scheduler) prepares written staffing schedules in advance. Each schedule shows name, position, shift and hours of every employee, and identifies the person in charge for each shift, so that at least the required number of staff is on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Staff scheduled for supervision may not leave the building to perform off-site duties unless the minimum on-site number remains present. A staff member counted in the minimum number may not be counted toward more than one function at the same time.

Personal care hours must be scheduled over both day and evening shifts. The schedule shows personal care assignments by shift. The food service schedule shows at least 35 hours per week even when the census is low.

At every shift change the outgoing shift lead confirms that the incoming staff are present before leaving. If a staff member calls out, the shift lead notifies the Administrator or designee at once, who arranges coverage (on-call list, overtime, agency staff) so the minimum is never breached. Mandatory staffing is never covered by a resident or by an employee under age 18.
Any employee under 18 may not have direct supervision responsibility for residents and may not work without on-site supervision by an adult employee.

Where the program is an ALR, the Administrator schedules a case manager on site for the minimum weekly hours required for the licensed capacity: at least 20 hours per week under 25 beds, scaling up to 40 hours per week at 45 or more beds. Case manager hours are posted in the schedule.

Where the program is an EALR or SNALR, the Administrator schedules an RN 8 hours per day, 5 days a week, and an LPN 8 hours per day on the other 2 days, with an RN on call 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. If the facility has 40 or fewer beds and relies on a DOH-approved waiver, a copy of the waiver and the alternate coverage plan are kept with the schedule. See HCS-03.
Where the program is an enriched housing program, the Administrator schedules a program coordinator and case manager hours as required by 488.9 and confirms the combined staff hours.
Where the program participates in the ALP, the Administrator keeps a designated individual and a qualified case manager as required by 494.6 and meets the 487.9 staffing minimums. See HCS-10.

Before admitting residents with special needs (e.g., dementia, SNALR) or when the census exceeds 200, the Administrator reviews whether additional staff are needed. DOH may require more staff than the minimums for a census over 200 or for special populations; the facility follows any such directive.

The Administrator compares actual hours worked (time records) to scheduled hours at least monthly. Any shortfall below the minimum is corrected in the next schedule and reported to the QA/QI Committee.

When a key position (Administrator, case manager, activities director, dietary consultant or health consultant) becomes vacant, the Administrator (or the governing body if the Administrator position is vacant) notifies the DOH regional office in writing within 3 business days and keeps a copy of the notice. The notice includes the position, date of vacancy and interim coverage. The facility also notifies the regional office when the position is filled.
Where the Administrator position is vacant, the governing body names an interim person who meets the requirements of GOV-02 and informs the regional office as directed.
The Administrator retains each written staffing schedule, and its revisions, for at least 12 months after the schedule's last date, and makes them available to DOH surveyors on request.
The QA/QI Committee reviews staffing compliance, call-outs and vacancies at least quarterly (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Provides budget and authority to staff to the required levels and appoints interim coverage if the Administrator position is vacant.
Calculates required staffing, approves schedules, ensures coverage, reports key vacancies within 3 business days, and keeps schedules for 12 months.
Prepares schedules in line with the staffing table and weekly hours and maintains the on-call list.
Confirms staffing at each shift, reports call-outs and does not leave until relieved.
Ensures RN/LPN coverage and 24/7 RN on-call availability.

documentation: Written staffing schedules and revisions (retained 12 months)
Weekly census-based staffing and hours calculation
Time and attendance records
Written notices of key-position vacancies and fills to the DOH regional office
On-call lists and EALR/SNALR waiver documents, if any
QA/QI Committee minutes on staffing

policies.title: Background Checks, Justice Center Staff Exclusion List and State Central Register
policies.applies_to: All applicants, employees, volunteers and contractors with direct resident contact; Administrator, HR/hiring staff
policies.purpose: To prevent the hiring or engagement of persons who are barred from working with vulnerable people, and to document each pre-hire screening before a person has direct contact with residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a facility subject to the Justice Center. Before hiring or engaging any person who will have direct contact with residents, the facility verifies through the Justice Center that the person is not on the Justice Center staff exclusion list. If the person is not on that list, the facility consults the State Central Register as required. A person on the staff exclusion list is never hired or engaged. A listing in the State Central Register is considered in the hiring decision but is not an automatic bar. The facility documents each check in the personnel file before the person has unsupervised resident contact (18 NYCRR 487.9(a)(7), (a)(17)). The facility also completes criminal history record checks as required by New York law, as confirmed by the facility's counsel.

definitions.definition: The list kept by the Justice Center of persons barred from positions with direct contact with people receiving services in covered facilities.
The register of reports of abuse and neglect maintained by the State; its consultation is required for certain employment screening and a listing is a factor, not a bar.
Any position in which the person provides services to residents or has regular, in-person access to residents, including volunteers and contracted workers.
Retained as a contractor, agency or temporary worker, or volunteer, whether paid or unpaid.

procedures: The Administrator designates a trained staff member (the HR designee) to complete and document all pre-hire checks. The designee has Justice Center system access as required and keeps log-in credentials confidential.
Job postings and applications state that employment is conditional on satisfactory checks. Each applicant signs a consent for the background checks before any check is run.

Before an offer becomes final and before the person has any direct contact with residents, the HR designee checks the Justice Center staff exclusion list through the Justice Center's process. The designee prints or saves the result with the date and the designee's name.

If the applicant is on the staff exclusion list, the facility does not hire or engage the person. The Administrator notifies the applicant that the offer cannot proceed, without sharing information with unrelated parties, and records the outcome.
If the applicant is not on the staff exclusion list, the HR designee consults the State Central Register as required and documents the result with the date.

If the State Central Register check shows a listing, the Administrator reviews the facts (nature of the finding, how long ago, relevance to the position, rehabilitation evidence and any information from the applicant) and decides in writing whether to hire. The listing is a factor but is not alone a bar. The written decision, with reasons, is kept in the personnel file. The Administrator consults counsel before applying any adverse decision.

The facility completes criminal history record checks for direct-care staff as required by applicable New York law. The Administrator confirms the exact legal authority and process with the facility's counsel and records that confirmation in the compliance file. Results are reviewed under the same individualized process, in line with New York law on considering criminal history.

The HR designee checks references and previous employment. For Administrator candidates, the facility obtains three recent letters of recommendation as required by 487.9(c)(9)(ii) and files them with the application.

No new hire, volunteer or contractor may be left alone with residents until all required checks are complete and cleared. Where a start date is pending a check, the person may not work in a resident-care role.

The facility rechecks the staff exclusion list for current direct-contact employees at the intervals set by the Justice Center and the facility's compliance plan, and at any time the Administrator learns of a concern. Any employee who is found to be on the list is removed from resident contact immediately.

Staff must immediately tell the Administrator if they are charged with or convicted of a crime or are named in an abuse or neglect report. The Administrator evaluates the matter, including whether to reassign the employee away from residents.

Contractors and agencies that supply staff with direct resident contact must confirm in writing that the Justice Center exclusion list check was done, or the facility runs the check itself before the person starts.
All check results are kept in a confidential section of the personnel file, separate from general personnel records where practical, and shared only with those who need to know (STF-06).
The QA/QI Committee receives an annual audit result showing that every direct-contact employee, volunteer and contractor has the required checks on file (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Makes final hiring decisions, reviews State Central Register listings and criminal history results, and ensures no one works with residents before checks clear.
Runs and documents each check, maintains the check log and files results in the personnel file.
Confirms the legal authority and procedure for criminal history checks and advises on adverse decisions.
Report charges, convictions or abuse/neglect reports naming them to the Administrator at once.

documentation: Signed applicant consent for checks
Dated Justice Center staff exclusion list verification for each person
Dated State Central Register consultation results and the Administrator's written decision where a listing exists
Criminal history record check results and the compliance file note on legal authority
Reference checks; three recommendation letters for the Administrator
Background check log and annual audit result

policies.title: Hiring, Orientation and Ongoing Training
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors with resident contact; Administrator, trainers, HR
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who works with residents is properly oriented before duties begin and receives documented ongoing training that keeps resident care safe and compliant.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives every employee and volunteer an initial orientation and ongoing in-service training as required by 18 NYCRR 487.9(a)(3)-(5) and, for the ALR, 10 NYCRR 1001.11(f)-(h). Orientation covers the characteristics and needs of the resident population, resident rights and facility rules, staff duties, the person's specific duties, emergency procedures, and Justice Center reportable incidents, reporting procedures and mandated reporter duties. The Justice Center code of conduct is given to each person at hire and every year, with a signed acknowledgment of receipt and understanding, and also to contractors with resident contact. In-service training continues throughout employment and is documented by date, time, topic, trainers and attendees. Each job has a written job description. Bloodborne pathogen training is given at hire and every year under 10 NYCRR 1001.11(h)(3) and the federal OSHA standard.

definitions.definition: Training given at hire, before the person works independently with residents, on the topics in this policy.
Ongoing training given during employment to maintain and update knowledge and skills.
The code issued by the Justice Center that sets expectations of conduct toward residents and is acknowledged by staff in writing.
A person required by law to report suspected abuse, neglect or other reportable incidents (see SAF-01).

procedures: Before hire, the Administrator or department head gives each applicant the written job description for the position. Job descriptions are kept current and reviewed annually. Each employee signs that they received their job description.

The HR designee confirms that required checks (STF-02) and health requirements (STF-05) are complete and that the applicant can speak, read and write English, as required for staff, before the person works with residents.

On or before the first day of work, and before any independent resident care, the trainer gives orientation covering: (a) characteristics and needs of the resident population (including dementia where applicable); (b) resident rights and facility rules; (c) staff duties; (d) the specific duties of the person's own job; and (e) emergency procedures.
For ALR staff, orientation also covers service procedures, response to emergencies, the evacuation and disaster plan (SAF-05, SAF-06), and personal appearance expectations.

Orientation also covers reportable incidents, reporting procedures and mandated reporter duties for the Justice Center and DOH, with the facility's hotline and reporting steps (SAF-01), and the facility's incident reporting process (SAF-02).

At hire, the HR designee gives the person the Justice Center code of conduct. The person signs an acknowledgment that they received and understand it. The same is done at least annually. Contractors with resident contact receive the code and sign the acknowledgment before starting.

Each employee receives bloodborne pathogen training at hire and at least yearly, covering the facility's exposure control and post-exposure procedures (SAF-07), consistent with the federal OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard.
Volunteers and any resident volunteer or resident employee receive orientation suited to their tasks, including resident rights, confidentiality and emergency procedures, before they begin.

New staff shadow an experienced staff member for the period set by the Administrator before working independently. A supervisor signs off in the personnel file when the new employee shows competence in assigned tasks.

Personal care staff complete the required training within 3 months of hire, under the in-service plan the facility has submitted to DOH. Resident aides follow STF-04. Staff who assist with medications follow HCS-02.

The Administrator develops an annual in-service training plan that includes resident rights, abuse and neglect prevention, infection control, fire safety, emergency procedures, dementia care, falls and skin care, and topics identified by incident reviews, QA/QI findings and staff feedback.
Staff take part in work-related training as required. Time spent in required training is paid time (STF-08).

For each training session, the trainer records date, time, topic, names and qualifications of the trainers, and a signed list of attendees. Sign-in sheets are filed in training records and a copy placed in each attendee's personnel file.

The Administrator runs a quarterly training report listing each employee's required training and due dates. Missed training is made up within 30 days, and the employee is not assigned tasks that require the missed training until completed.
The Administrator reviews the training program annually with the QA/QI Committee and updates it after regulatory changes, serious incidents or survey findings (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures orientation and in-service training are provided, documented and current; maintains job descriptions.
Tracks training due dates, collects Justice Center code of conduct acknowledgments, and files training records.
Deliver and document orientation and in-service; observe and sign off on competence.
Attend required training, sign acknowledgments and apply training to daily work.
Teaches or supervises clinical topics and bloodborne pathogen training where applicable.

documentation: Signed written job descriptions
Orientation checklists with topics, date, trainer and employee signature
Signed Justice Center code of conduct acknowledgments (at hire and annually; contractors)
Training sign-in sheets with date, time, topic, trainers and attendees
Bloodborne pathogen training records (hire and annual)
Annual in-service plan and quarterly training compliance report

policies.title: Resident Aide Training and Competency (ALR)
policies.applies_to: Resident aides and home health aides in the Assisted Living Residence, including EALR and SNALR; Administrator, nurse, trainers
policies.purpose: To make sure resident aides in the ALR complete required initial and ongoing training and are assessed for competence at least once each year.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires each ALR resident aide to complete 40 hours of initial training under the DOH curriculum or an approved equivalent, 12 hours of ongoing in-service training every year on topics relevant to their responsibilities, and an annual performance assessment that includes at least one direct observation (10 NYCRR 1001.11(c)(2)). Training records are kept in each aide's personnel file. In an EALR or SNALR, home health aides meet the applicable DOH home health aide training requirements, plus first aid and medication assistance training, and complete 12 hours of annual in-service training.

definitions.definition: A staff member who provides personal care and related help to ALR residents under the facility's service procedures and supervision.
The 40-hour training under the DOH curriculum or an approved equivalent that must be completed as required before the aide independently provides care.
At least 12 hours each year on topics relevant to the aide's responsibilities.
An evaluator's in-person observation of the aide performing resident care tasks, documented as part of the annual performance assessment.
An aide who provides home health aide tasks under nursing supervision in an EALR or SNALR.

procedures: At hire, the HR designee identifies whether the person is a resident aide or an EALR/SNALR home health aide and records any training the person has already completed, including certificates.

The Administrator or nurse reviews prior training. Prior training is accepted only if it matches the DOH curriculum or an approved equivalent and is documented. The reviewer records the decision in the personnel file.

Resident aides who have not completed the 40-hour initial training complete it using the DOH curriculum or approved equivalent program. The facility documents the hours, dates, topics, instructors and the aide's participation.

Until the aide completes initial training, the aide does not independently perform tasks for which the training is required. The aide works only under direct supervision of a qualified staff member, and the supervisor documents this.

The nurse or Administrator assesses and documents each aide's competence in required tasks before the aide independently performs them, including transfers, bathing, toileting, skin care observation, falls prevention, infection control, and emergency response.

For EALR/SNALR home health aides, the Administrator confirms completion of the applicable DOH home health aide training, first aid training and medication assistance training before the aide provides those services. Medication assistance tasks are limited by HCS-02, and nursing delegation follows HCS-03.

The Administrator schedules at least 12 hours of in-service training for each aide every year. Topics relate to the aide's responsibilities, such as resident rights, dementia care, personal care, falls, skin integrity, infection control, medication assistance limits and abuse prevention. Hours from STF-03 orientation and sessions are counted only if they are relevant to the aide's responsibilities.
The HR designee tracks each aide's anniversary and in-service hours monthly and notifies the Administrator when an aide is behind schedule. Missing hours are made up within 30 days.

At least once a year, a qualified supervisor (nurse or Administrator-designated evaluator) completes a written performance assessment for each aide. The assessment includes at least one direct observation of the aide providing care to a resident, using the facility's competency checklist.

The evaluator reviews the assessment with the aide, including strengths and areas for improvement. Both sign the assessment. Where weaknesses are found, the evaluator sets a written corrective plan with retraining and a follow-up observation within 30 days.
An aide who fails to complete required training or who is found not competent is removed from the affected duties until retrained and re-evaluated.
The HR designee files all training certificates, hour logs and assessments in the aide's personnel file as required (STF-06) and keeps the file available for DOH review.
The Administrator reports training completion rates and assessment results to the QA/QI Committee at least annually (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all aides complete initial training, 12 annual in-service hours and the annual assessment; removes untrained aides from affected duties.
Assesses competence, conducts direct observations and supervises home health aides in the EALR/SNALR.
Tracks hours and due dates and files training records.
Complete required training, perform only tasks they are trained for and take part in annual assessment.

documentation: Certificates and record of the 40-hour initial training
In-service sign-in sheets and annual hours log (12 hours)
Annual performance assessment with documented direct observation and signatures
Competency checklists and corrective plans
EALR/SNALR home health aide, first aid and medication assistance training records

policies.title: Employee Health Assessment and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees and volunteers with resident contact; Administrator, HR designee, health consultant/nurse
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff by confirming that each employee is physically and mentally able to do their work, and that employees are screened for tuberculosis and other communicable disease risks.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] obtains a health assessment for each employee at hire and at least every 12 months, and performs TB screening before employment and annually, as required by 18 NYCRR 487.9(a)(8)-(11).
